children.title: Assignment Direction
children.top_down_role: The primary distinction between selective output maximization and compulsory-demand input minimization.

children.title: Knapsack Assignment Regime
children.top_down_role: The classification route leading to knapsack families.

children.title: Output Maximization
children.top_down_role: Problem families organized around maximizing the value obtained from limited capacity.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many items with weights \(w_i\ge 0\) and values \(v_i\in\mathbb{R}\).
A single knapsack has scalar capacity \(C\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal solution is any \(x^*\in\arg\max\{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).
review_flags: Authoritative source specific to knapsack output maximization is missing from the supplied inventory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The binary single-knapsack output-maximization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an item set \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), output maximization selects a feasible subset of items having greatest total value. Equivalently, it is the optimization problem \[\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C\right\}.\] Items not selected consume no capacity and contribute no value; the number and capacity of knapsacks are fixed rather than decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a subset of items whose total weight fits one fixed knapsack and whose total value is maximum.
knowledge_statements.title: Output Maximization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary single-knapsack formulation is mathematically standard and fits the Output Maximization leaf, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports it.

children.title: Item Selection
children.top_down_role: Problem families whose central decision is the choice of admitted items.

assumptions_latex: The item set \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is finite.
Each item is indivisible and may be used at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissible selection vectors are exactly \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), with selected set \(S(x)=\{i\in I:x_i=1\}\).

notation.meaning: subset encoded by a selection vector

review_flags: Authoritative source specific to binary knapsack selection is missing from the supplied inventory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Item selection in the zero-one knapsack regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Item selection represents each indivisible item \(i\in I\) by a binary variable \(x_i\), where \(x_i=1\) means that item \(i\) is assigned to the knapsack and \(x_i=0\) means that it is omitted. Thus every decision vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) encodes the subset \[S(x)=\{i\in I:x_i=1\}.\] Feasibility is subsequently imposed by capacity or other assignment constraints on this encoded subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-one decision is made for every indivisible item, so each feasible vector encodes the subset placed in the knapsack.
knowledge_statements.title: Item Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary encoding of item selection is standard and the definition kind fits this leaf, but the record has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Knapsack Classification Route
children.top_down_role: The joint objective-assignment profile leading from the classification to knapsack families.

assumptions_latex: The instance has one fixed-capacity receiving object.
Available heterogeneous items are optional and carry additive rewards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Such an instance is classified on the knapsack route and has canonical form \(\max\{\sum_i v_i x_i:\sum_i w_i x_i\le C,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\}\).

notation.meaning: fixed capacity of the receiving object

review_flags: A cutting-and-packing taxonomy source supporting this classification criterion is not supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification criterion for the canonical zero-one knapsack branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A selection-packing instance follows the knapsack classification route when the receiving side consists of one object with fixed scalar capacity \(C\), each candidate item \(i\) is optional and used at most once, and the objective maximizes additive output from selected items. Its canonical formulation is \[\max\left\{\sum_i v_i x_i:\sum_i w_i x_i\le C,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] The defining direction is selection into a fixed object, not minimization of the number of objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify an instance as knapsack when optional rewarded items are selected for one fixed-capacity object and total reward is maximized.
knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Classification Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly describes the canonical zero-one knapsack route, but the asserted taxonomy criterion requires a cutting-and-packing source with a specific locator.

children.title: Packing-Cutting Assignment Regime
children.top_down_role: The classification route leading to bin-packing and cutting-stock families.

children.title: Input Minimization
children.top_down_role: Problem families organized around minimizing the stock objects or containers consumed.

assumptions_latex: Available large objects are identical and have scalar capacity \(C>0\).
Required items or demand quantities must be accommodated completely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input minimization seeks \(\min\{\sum_j y_j:\text{all demand is assigned feasibly and object }j\text{ is usable only if }y_j=1\}\).
review_flags: Authoritative cutting-and-packing source for the input-minimization classification is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization of identical large objects consumed by packing or cutting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input minimization fixes the required small-item demand and chooses how many large objects are consumed to satisfy it. For a sufficiently large index set \(J\) of candidate objects, binary variables \(y_j\) indicate use, and the objective is \[\min\sum_{j\in J}y_j.\] Assignment or cutting-pattern variables must accommodate every required item or demand unit, and no load assigned to object \(j\) may exceed \(C y_j\). The output demand is fixed; the quantity of input stock or bins is optimized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Meet all prescribed demand while minimizing the number of bins or stock objects consumed.
knowledge_statements.title: Input Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The input-minimization description fits the leaf, but no authoritative source supports the classification, and the phrase “sufficiently large index set” should be checked against a precise formulation.

children.title: Demand Accommodation
children.top_down_role: Problem families requiring specified items or production demands to be accommodated.

assumptions_latex: Each item type \(i\) has required integer demand \(d_i\ge 0\).
Every feasible object pattern contains nonnegative integer quantities \(a_{ip}\) of each type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Demand is accommodated exactly when \(\sum_p a_{ip}z_p\ge d_i\) for every item type \(i\).

notation.meaning: number of type-\(i\) pieces supplied by pattern \(p\)

review_flags: Authoritative source for the stated demand-covering convention is missing.
The distinction between covering and exact fulfillment should receive source review.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pattern-based covering convention allowing surplus production.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the set of feasible packing or cutting patterns for one large object. If pattern \(p\in P\) supplies \(a_{ip}\) units of item type \(i\) and is used \(z_p\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) times, prescribed demand \(d_i\) is accommodated when \[\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}z_p\ge d_i\qquad\text{for every }i.\] The inequality permits overproduction; a no-surplus convention replaces it by equality when exact fulfillment is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected packing or cutting patterns must collectively supply at least the prescribed quantity of every demanded item type.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand Accommodation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covering condition is coherent and explicitly distinguishes surplus-permitting coverage from exact fulfillment, but a source is needed to establish which convention belongs in this taxonomy leaf.

children.title: Bin-Packing Classification Route
children.top_down_role: The input-minimization route associated with packing prescribed items into containers.

assumptions_latex: Each individual item \(i\) has size \(0<w_i\le C\).
An unlimited collection of identical bins of capacity \(C\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance follows the bin-packing route when every item must be assigned once and the objective is to minimize the number of nonempty bins.
review_flags: A bin-packing textbook locator is absent from the supplied source inventory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification criterion for one-dimensional identical-bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A one-dimensional instance follows the bin-packing classification route when its input lists individual, strongly heterogeneous items, every item must be packed exactly once, bins are identical with capacity \(C\), and the objective minimizes used bins. A packing is a map \(b:I\to\{1,
\ldots,m\}\) satisfying \[\sum_{i:b(i)=j}w_i\le C\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m),\] and the optimization criterion is the smallest feasible \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify an instance as bin packing when individual items must all enter identical bins and the number of used bins is minimized.
knowledge_statements.title: Bin-Packing Classification Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is a standard one-dimensional bin-packing characterization and fits the classification-route leaf, but it lacks a supporting textbook citation and locator.

children.title: Cutting-Stock Classification Route
children.top_down_role: The demand-accommodation route associated with producing required piece multiplicities from stock.

assumptions_latex: Identical stock objects have length \(C>0\).
Item types have lengths \(0<w_i\le C\) and integer demands \(d_i\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance follows the cutting-stock route when feasible patterns cover type demands and \(\sum_p z_p\) is minimized.

notation.meaning: number of stock objects cut with pattern \(p\)

review_flags: A cutting-stock textbook locator is absent from the supplied source inventory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification criterion for one-dimensional cutting stock with typed demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional instance follows the cutting-stock classification route when identical stock objects are cut into demanded item types, many copies of a type may be required, and stock consumption is minimized. Each feasible pattern \(p\) satisfies \(\sum_i w_i a_{ip}\le C\). The canonical model is \[\min\left\{\sum_p z_p:\sum_p a_{ip}z_p\ge d_i\ \text{for every }i,\ z_p\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify an instance as cutting stock when typed piece demands are cut from identical stock and the number of stock objects is minimized.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Stock Classification Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pattern model is a standard cutting-stock formulation and the condition kind fits the route leaf, but neither the classification nor the covering convention has cited support.

children.title: Object-Item Assortment Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Assortment structure separating single-object selection, strongly heterogeneous packing, and weakly heterogeneous production.

children.title: Single Large Object with Strongly Heterogeneous Items
children.top_down_role: The canonical knapsack position in the cutting-and-packing taxonomy.

assumptions_latex: There is exactly one large object of scalar capacity \(C\).
Candidate items may have arbitrary item-specific sizes and rewards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The taxonomy position is the single-knapsack regime \(\max\{\sum_i v_i x_i:\sum_i w_i x_i\le C,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\}\).

notation.meaning: size and reward of heterogeneous item \(i\)
capacity of the unique large object

review_flags: A source defining the strong-heterogeneity taxonomy terminology is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional knapsack position in the assortment taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The combination of one large object and strongly heterogeneous items is represented by a unique capacity constraint with item-specific data. In the canonical binary case, the model is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Strong heterogeneity means that items are distinguished individually by their sizes, rewards, or both, rather than being specified only through a small collection of high-multiplicity demand types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One fixed object plus individually distinct optional items gives the canonical knapsack position in the taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.title: Single Large Object with Strongly Heterogeneous Items

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation matches the stated canonical knapsack position, but the meaning of “strongly heterogeneous items” and its asserted taxonomy placement require a specifically located source.

children.title: Identical Bins with Strongly Heterogeneous Items
children.top_down_role: The canonical one-dimensional bin-packing position.

assumptions_latex: All bins have the same scalar capacity \(C\).
Every strongly heterogeneous item \(i\) has an individual size \(0<w_i\le C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The taxonomy position is one-dimensional bin packing: minimize \(m\) subject to assigning every item once and respecting capacity in each of the \(m\) bins.
review_flags: A source defining the strong-heterogeneity taxonomy terminology is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional bin-packing position in the assortment taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Identical bins with strongly heterogeneous items are represented by individually listed item sizes and a variable number of equal-capacity bins. The canonical model seeks the least \(m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) for which there is an assignment \(b:I\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\) satisfying \[\sum_{i:b(i)=j}w_i\le C\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).\] Every item is mandatory and appears once; heterogeneity lies on the item side, while the large objects are interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Individually distinct mandatory items packed into a minimum number of equal-capacity bins form the canonical one-dimensional bin-packing position.
knowledge_statements.title: Identical Bins with Strongly Heterogeneous Items

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically consistent with one-dimensional bin packing, but the strong-heterogeneity terminology and taxonomy position are unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Identical Stock with Weakly Heterogeneous Demands
children.top_down_role: The canonical one-dimensional cutting-stock position.

assumptions_latex: All stock objects have the same length \(C\).
Demand is aggregated into item types with lengths \(w_i\) and multiplicities \(d_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The taxonomy position is one-dimensional cutting stock: minimize stock usage over patterns satisfying \(\sum_i w_i a_{ip}\le C\) and covering every \(d_i\).

notation.meaning: length and required multiplicity of type \(i\)

review_flags: A source defining weak heterogeneity in the cutting-and-packing taxonomy is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional cutting-stock position with aggregated demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Identical stock with weakly heterogeneous demands is represented by a set of item types rather than a list of individually distinguished pieces. Type \(i\) has length \(w_i\) and multiplicity demand \(d_i\), while every stock object has length \(C\). Feasible patterns satisfy \(\sum_i w_i a_{ip}\le C\), and nonnegative integer pattern counts \(z_p\) are chosen to minimize \(\sum_p z_p\) subject to \[\sum_p a_{ip}z_p\ge d_i\qquad\text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A few demanded piece types with multiplicities cut from identical stock form the canonical one-dimensional cutting-stock position.
knowledge_statements.title: Identical Stock with Weakly Heterogeneous Demands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pattern representation is consistent with cutting stock, but the interpretation of weak heterogeneity and the canonical taxonomy placement need authoritative, specifically located support.

children.title: Model-Scope Boundary
children.top_down_role: The chapter develops scalar-capacity models; spatial layouts and integrated production systems are routed elsewhere.

children.title: Scalar Capacity-Cutting Core
children.top_down_role: Scalar-capacity problems developed within this chapter.

children.title: One-Dimensional Capacity Models
children.top_down_role: Scalar-capacity selection or packing models developed within the chapter.

assumptions_latex: Every item consumes a nonnegative scalar amount \(w_i\).
Each receiving object has scalar capacity \(C_j\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A placement \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(\sum_i w_i x_{ij}\le C_j\) for every receiving object \(j\), together with the model's assignment constraints.

notation.meaning: indicator that item \(i\) is assigned to object \(j\)

review_flags: A source specific to one-dimensional packing-capacity models is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive scalar-capacity models without geometric placement variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional capacity model represents each item by one scalar size and each receiving object by one scalar capacity. For assignment variables \(x_{ij}\), the load condition on object \(j\) is \[\sum_i w_i x_{ij}\le C_j.\] Feasibility depends only on additive scalar consumption and the relevant selection or assignment restrictions. No coordinates, orientations, shapes, or nonoverlap constraints are present, so any two placements with the same assigned item sets are equivalent in this model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Items consume additive scalar capacity; feasibility is determined by load inequalities and assignment rules, without geometric placement decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Capacity Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive scalar-capacity definition fits the one-dimensional capacity-model leaf and is internally coherent, but it has no supporting source or locator.

children.title: One-Dimensional Cutting Models
children.top_down_role: Scalar stock-cutting families governed by piece lengths and stock lengths.

assumptions_latex: Each stock object is a line segment of length \(C>0\).
Each demanded piece type \(i\) has length \(w_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cutting pattern is feasible exactly when \(a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^n\) and \(\sum_i w_i a_i\le C\).

notation.meaning: number of type-\(i\) pieces in a pattern

review_flags: A source specific to one-dimensional cutting-pattern models is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-length cutting patterns without kerf or geometric complications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional cutting model describes one stock object by its length \(C\) and a cutting pattern by a vector \(a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^n\), where \(a_i\) is the number of pieces of length \(w_i\). The pattern is feasible precisely when \[\sum_{i=1}^n w_i a_i\le C.\] The unused remainder is \(C-\sum_i w_i a_i\). This core model neglects kerf, trim requirements, sequencing, and higher-dimensional geometry unless additional constraints explicitly introduce them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting pattern specifies integer piece counts whose total length does not exceed the length of one stock object.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Cutting Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integer cutting-pattern definition fits the one-dimensional cutting-model leaf and clearly states its exclusions, but no cited source with a specific locator supports it.

children.title: Scalar Capacity Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary separating the chapter core from vector-capacity or spatial-placement families.

assumptions_latex: Item sizes and the capacity are nonnegative scalars: \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\) and \(C\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership is determined solely by the scalar inequality \(\sum_i a_i x_i\le C\); models requiring multiple resource coordinates or spatial nonoverlap lie outside this boundary.

notation.meaning: selected multiplicity of item type i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distinction between one-resource capacity models, vector-capacity models, and geometric packing
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates scalar capacity feasibility from multi-resource and geometric placement models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A selection-packing-cutting model belongs to the scalar-capacity core when every item type \(i\) has one scalar size \(a_i\), the container or stock object has one scalar capacity \(C\), and feasibility of a selection \(x\) is characterized by \[\sum_i a_i x_i\le C.\] Side constraints on multiplicities may be present, but feasibility must not require a vector of independent capacities, item coordinates, orientations, or pairwise spatial nonoverlap. Introducing any such essential requirement crosses the scalar-capacity boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is scalar-capacity precisely when one additive capacity inequality determines packing feasibility; essential multiple resources or spatial placement move it outside this class.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Capacity Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the proposed classification criterion, and the domain of the multiplicities x_i is not specified.

children.title: Vector-Capacity Extensions
children.top_down_role: Nongeometric multi-resource extensions retained only where they preserve the chapter's combinatorial structure.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many item types and resource coordinates, with \(a_{ri}\ge0\) and \(b_r\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is the integer optimization problem \(\max\{p^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in X\}\), where no geometric placement variables are required.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard multidimensional-knapsack and vector-packing formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers additive multi-resource selection without geometric placement constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector-capacity extension has item types \(i=1,\ldots,n\), resources \(r=1,\ldots,d\), profits \(p_i\), consumption vectors \(a_i=(a_{1i},\ldots,a_{di})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}\), and capacity \(b\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}\). Its canonical form is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ri}x_i\le b_r\ \text{for every }r,\ x\in X\right\},\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n}\) supplies multiplicity restrictions. The extension remains nongeometric when these coordinatewise additive inequalities completely express packing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector-capacity models select integer item multiplicities subject to several additive resource limits, while retaining no coordinates, orientations, or spatial nonoverlap decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Vector-Capacity Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the nongeometric multi-resource topic, but it has no citation and does not specify the domain of the profits p_i.

children.title: Geometric Placement Family
children.top_down_role: Two- and three-dimensional placement families rehomed to geometric packing.

children.title: Spatial Packing
children.top_down_role: Two-dimensional or three-dimensional placement families routed to geometric packing.

assumptions_latex: Each item and container is a compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) with nonempty interior.
A specified family of admissible rigid motions is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A packing is feasible exactly when every transformed item lies in its assigned container and transformed interiors are pairwise disjoint within each container.

notation.meaning: geometric region occupied by item i
admissible rigid motion applied to item i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard containment-and-nonoverlap definition of geometric packing
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses exact geometric containment and interior nonoverlap in fixed-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given item regions \(S_1,\ldots,S_n\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and container regions \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\), a spatial packing chooses an assignment \(k(i)\) and an admissible rigid motion \(T_i\) for every packed item. It is feasible when \[T_i(S_i)\subseteq B_{k(i)}\quad\text{for every }i,\] and \[\operatorname{int}(T_i(S_i))\cap\operatorname{int}(T_j(S_j))=\varnothing\] whenever \(i\ne j\) and \(k(i)=k(j)\). The optimization criterion may minimize used containers or maximize packed value, area, or volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spatial packing assigns moved geometric items to containers so that each item is contained and no two assigned items overlap in their interiors.
knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Packing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and containment/nonoverlap conditions fit Spatial Packing, but no source is cited and the assignment map k is not given an explicit domain and codomain.

children.title: Strip Packing
children.top_down_role: Packing families with a fixed cross-section and an extent to be minimized.

assumptions_latex: The strip has fixed width \(W>0\) and unbounded length.
Items are compact planar regions with specified admissible orientations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the least \(H\) for which all transformed items fit in \([0,W]\times[0,H]\) with pairwise disjoint interiors.

notation.meaning: admissibly transformed region of item i

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the two-dimensional fixed-width, minimum-used-length version.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compact planar items \(S_1,\ldots,S_n\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\) and a strip of fixed width \(W>0\), strip packing chooses an admissible rigid motion \(T_i\) for each item and a used length \(H\ge0\). The problem is \[\min H\] subject to \[T_i(S_i)\subseteq[0,W]\times[0,H]\quad\text{for every }i\] and \[\operatorname{int}(T_i(S_i))\cap\operatorname{int}(T_j(S_j))=\varnothing\quad\text{for }i\ne j.\] For rectangular variants, admissible orientations may be fixed or restricted to rotations by \(90\) degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strip packing places all items without overlap in a fixed-width, unbounded-length strip and minimizes the length occupied.
knowledge_statements.title: Strip Packing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-width minimum-length formulation and definition kind fit Strip Packing, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

children.title: Nesting Problems
children.top_down_role: Irregular-shape placement families routed to geometric nesting coverage.

assumptions_latex: Item and stock boundaries are represented by compact planar regions.
The admissible translations and rotations are specified for each item.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires containment in the stock region and pairwise interior disjointness; optimization minimizes stock usage or waste.

notation.meaning: possibly irregular planar shape of item i
admissible translation and rotation of item i

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers irregular two-dimensional shapes under prescribed translations and rotations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nesting problem is a geometric packing problem for possibly nonrectangular item regions \(S_i\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\). A solution chooses admissible transformations \(T_i\) and, when several stock pieces are available, an assignment of items to stock regions. For each assigned pair it requires \[T_i(S_i)\subseteq B,\] while distinct items sharing stock must satisfy \[\operatorname{int}(T_i(S_i))\cap\operatorname{int}(T_j(S_j))=\varnothing.\] Typical objectives minimize the number or total length of stock pieces, or equivalently minimize unused stock area under a fixed stock configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nesting places irregular planar shapes within stock, allowing prescribed rotations and translations while enforcing containment and nonoverlap and minimizing stock use or waste.
knowledge_statements.title: Nesting Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Nesting Problems, but no source is cited, multiple stock regions are discussed while only B is defined, and minimizing unused area is not generally equivalent to the other listed objectives under a fixed stock configuration.

children.title: Production-Planning Coupling Family
children.top_down_role: Operational couplings rehomed to production-planning chapters.

children.title: Integrated Lot-Sizing Models
children.top_down_role: Cutting or packing models coupled to production-quantity decisions.

assumptions_latex: Demand \(d_{it}\ge0\) is given for every item type \(i\) and period \(t\).
Each cutting or packing pattern has a known output vector and period-dependent usage cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility couples pattern production to the inventory balance \(I_{i,t-1}+\sum_p a_{ip}y_{pt}=d_{it}+I_{it}\), with setup or lot decisions restricting \(y_{pt}\).

notation.meaning: uses of pattern p in period t
units of item i produced by pattern p

children.title: Zero-One Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Binary item-selection instances.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) items with weights \(w_i\ge0\), profits \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and capacity \(C\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible decisions are exactly the binary vectors satisfying \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le C\), and the objective is \(p^{\mathsf T}x\).

notation.meaning: weight and profit of item i
binary indicator that item i is selected

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard single-constraint profit-maximization formulation.

source_refs.locator: Section 5. Some Apparently Nonpolynomial-Bounded Problems p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero-one knapsack problem is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i x_i\le C,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.\] Each item may be selected at most once. A vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) is feasible precisely when its total weight does not exceed \(C\); its objective value is the total profit of the selected items.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-one knapsack selects each item at most once to maximize total profit without exceeding one scalar weight capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-One Knapsack

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5. Some Apparently Nonpolynomial-Bounded Problems p. 8

children.title: Bounded Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Finite item-multiplicity instances.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) item types with weights \(w_i\ge0\), profits \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), finite bounds \(u_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\), and capacity \(C\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible multiplicities satisfy \(0\le x_i\le u_i\) and \(\sum_i w_i x_i\le C\), with objective \(\sum_i p_i x_i\).

notation.meaning: weight and profit of item type i
available multiplicity of item type i
selected multiplicity of item type i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses finite, item-specific integer multiplicity bounds.

source_refs.locator: Section 5. Some Apparently Nonpolynomial-Bounded Problems p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded knapsack problem is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i x_i\le C,\ x_i\in\mathbb{Z},\ 0\le x_i\le u_i\ \text{for every }i\right\}.\] Here \(u_i<\infty\) is the available number of copies of item type \(i\). Thus feasibility combines one scalar capacity inequality with finite type-specific multiplicity bounds; the zero-one case is obtained when \(u_i=1\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded knapsack chooses an integer number of copies of each item type, up to a finite bound, to maximize profit under one capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Knapsack

children.title: Subset-Sum Attainability
children.top_down_role: Binary selection instances centered on whether a target total is attainable.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Sum Attainability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision predicate for finite nonnegative-integer subset sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and a target \(B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), the target is subset-sum attainable precisely when
\[
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i=B.
\]
Equivalently, \(B\) belongs to the finite set \(\left\{\sum_{i\in S}a_i:S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\right\}\). The associated decision problem returns YES exactly under this predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target is attainable when some subset of the given positive integers sums exactly to it.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\)
\(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for every \(i\)
\(B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is attainable}\iff\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i=B\).

notation.meaning: binary indicator that item i is selected

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite subset-sum decision predicate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically precise and fits Subset-Sum Attainability, but no inspectable citation or authoritative locator is supplied.

children.title: Exact-Fill Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection instances requiring capacity or demand to be met exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Fill Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-maximizing binary selection with an exact capacity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For item weights \(a_i\), profits \(p_i\), and prescribed fill level \(B\), the exact-fill selection problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i=B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.
\]
If no binary vector satisfies the equality, the instance is infeasible. Unlike ordinary packing knapsack, unused capacity is forbidden; feasibility is exactly subset-sum attainability for the weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a subset having total weight exactly equal to capacity and, among such subsets, maximize total profit.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) and \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(p_i\in\mathbb R\)
\(B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{p^\top x:a^\top x=B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\), when this set is nonempty.

notation.meaning: weight and profit of item i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical exact-capacity binary knapsack formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently describes profit maximization subject to exact binary fill, but it has no inspectable supporting source.

children.title: Target-Equality Boundary
children.top_down_role: The distinction between exact target attainment and ordinary capacity-feasible selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Equality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality cannot generally be replaced by either one-sided knapsack inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative weights, the equality constraint \(a^\top x=B\) is equivalent to imposing both \(a^\top x\le B\) and \(a^\top x\ge B\). Either inequality alone changes attainability. With one item of weight \(2\) and target \(1\), the packing relaxation \(2x\le1\) admits \(x=0\), while the covering relaxation \(2x\ge1\) admits \(x=1\); nevertheless neither binary choice satisfies \(2x=1\). Thus one-sided feasibility does not certify exact target attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact attainment requires both packing and covering inequalities; either inequality alone can be feasible when equality is impossible.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\)
\(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^\top x=B\iff(a^\top x\le B\ \wedge\ a^\top x\ge B)\), but neither conjunct alone implies equality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary equality decomposition with explicit binary counterexample

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary and counterexample are correct and appropriately scoped, but the record supplies no citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Change-Making Problems
children.top_down_role: Exact-value and minimum-cardinality arithmetic variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Change-Making Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded exact-value change making with minimum coin cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given positive integer denominations \(d_1,\ldots,d_m\) and target value \(B\), the minimum-cardinality change-making problem is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m y_j:\sum_{j=1}^m d_jy_j=B,\ y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\right\}.
\]
The instance is feasible exactly when \(B\) belongs to the nonnegative integer semigroup generated by the denominations. If feasible, an optimizer specifies the number of coins of each denomination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent the target exactly using unlimited coins of given denominations while minimizing the total number of coins.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\)
\(d_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for every \(j\)
\(B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{\mathbf1^\top y:d^\top y=B,\ y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\}\), when feasible.

notation.meaning: number of coins of denomination j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard unbounded minimum-coin change-making formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record precisely defines the unbounded minimum-coin change-making variant named in the scope, but no authoritative source or locator supports that selected variant.

children.title: Minimum-Covering Knapsack Pair
children.top_down_role: Covering-oriented counterparts of value maximization.

children.title: Minimum Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants minimizing resource use or cost while meeting a prescribed target.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary minimum-cost selection meeting a single benefit demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given nonnegative item costs \(c_i\), nonnegative benefits \(a_i\), and demand \(B\), the minimum knapsack problem is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\ge B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.
\]
The problem is infeasible when \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i<B\). Otherwise, an optimum is a demand-covering subset of minimum total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-cost subset whose accumulated benefit reaches or exceeds a required demand.
assumptions_latex: \(c,a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\)
\(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{c^\top x:a^\top x\ge B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\), when feasible.

notation.meaning: benefit or coverage supplied by item i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary minimum-cost covering formulation is internally correct and fits the stated Minimum Knapsack sense, but it lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Covering Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants organized around satisfying a covering requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-row binary covering model with additive selection cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A covering-knapsack instance has feasible set
\[
K_{\mathrm{cov}}=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\ge B\right\},
\]
where each coefficient \(a_i\) is nonnegative and \(B\) is the required coverage. With nonnegative costs \(c_i\), its optimization form minimizes \(c^\top x\) over \(K_{\mathrm{cov}}\). Oversupply is permitted, but any selected subset supplying less than \(B\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering knapsack selects items whose total coverage meets a threshold, commonly minimizing their total cost.
assumptions_latex: \(a,c\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\)
\(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{cov}}=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:a^\top x\ge B\}\) and the minimum-cost value is \(\min_{x\in K_{\mathrm{cov}}}c^\top x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard single-row binary covering formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-set definition and minimum-cost form are consistent with single-row binary covering knapsack, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Minimum-Covering Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The relationship between target-constrained minimization and covering-oriented formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Covering Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum knapsack represented as minimum-cost optimization over a covering-knapsack set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For common data \(a,c\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\) and \(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), define \(K_{\mathrm{cov}}=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:a^\top x\ge B\}\). Then the minimum-knapsack value and the minimum-cost covering-knapsack value coincide:
\[
\min\{c^\top x:a^\top x\ge B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}=\min\{c^\top x:x\in K_{\mathrm{cov}}\}.
\]
Their feasible solutions and optimal solutions are identical under the identity mapping of item variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum knapsack is precisely minimum-cost optimization over the corresponding binary covering-knapsack feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(a,c\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\)
\(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
\(K_{\mathrm{cov}}\ne\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{a^\top x\ge B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n}c^\top x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K_{\mathrm{cov}}}c^\top x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality follows from the identical feasible set and objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly identifies the two formulations through their identical feasible set and objective, but the claimed nomenclatural correspondence is uncited.

children.title: Generalized Knapsack Structure Taxonomy

children.title: Multidimensional Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Selection under several resource coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary profit maximization under several resource capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given profits \(p_i\), resource consumptions \(a_{ji}\), and capacities \(b_j\), the \(m\)-dimensional binary knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ji}x_i\le b_j\ \text{for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,m\},\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.
\]
Each selected item simultaneously consumes capacity in every resource coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize selected profit while respecting a separate capacity constraint for each of several resources.

\(A\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^m\)
\(p\in\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{p^\top x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

children.title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Grouped alternatives with class-level selection restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactly-one-per-class version of grouped binary knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_q\) partition the item set. The exactly-one multiple-choice knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le B,\ \sum_{i\in G_k}x_i=1\ \text{for every }k,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.
\]
Thus one alternative is selected from each class while the total weight remains within capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose exactly one item from every class, respecting a common capacity, to maximize total profit.
assumptions_latex: \(G_1,\ldots,G_q\) are nonempty and partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\) and \(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
\(p\in\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{p^\top x:a^\top x\le B,\ \sum_{i\in G_k}x_i=1\ \forall k,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: weight and profit of item i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exactly-one multiple-choice knapsack variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exactly-one-per-class formulation is mathematically coherent, but multiple-choice knapsack also has at-most-one conventions; an authoritative locator is needed to substantiate this selected variant.

children.title: Multiple Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Selection and assignment across several containers.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary item assignment to multiple capacitated knapsacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For items with weights \(a_i\), profits \(p_i\), and knapsack capacities \(B_k\), the multiple-knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{k=1}^m\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_{ik}:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_{ik}\le B_k\ \forall k,\ \sum_{k=1}^m x_{ik}\le1\ \forall i,\ x_{ik}\in\{0,1\}\right\}.
\]
An item may be assigned to at most one knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each item to at most one of several capacitated knapsacks to maximize the profit of assigned items.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\)
\(a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\) and \(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^m\)
\(p\in\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) maximizes \(\sum_{k,i}p_i x_{ik}\) subject to the capacity and unique-assignment constraints.

notation.meaning: indicator that item i is assigned to knapsack k
weight and profit of item i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assignment and capacity formulation correctly distinguishes multiple knapsacks from multidimensional knapsack, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Item-Relation Knapsack Family
children.top_down_role: Variants with interactions or admissibility relations among items.

children.title: Quadratic Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants with pairwise contributions in the objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary knapsack with pairwise interaction terms in the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given capacity data \(a,B\), linear profits \(p\), and interaction coefficients \(q_{ij}\), the quadratic knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}x_ix_j:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.
\]
The term \(q_{ij}\) contributes only when both items \(i\) and \(j\) are selected; it may represent synergy or a penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize linear item profit plus pairwise interaction values while the selected items satisfy one capacity constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\) and \(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
\(p\in\mathbb R^n\)
\(q_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for \(i<j\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{a^\top x\le B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left(\sum_i p_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}q_{ij}x_ix_j\right)\).

notation.meaning: joint value of selecting items i and j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard pairwise-objective quadratic knapsack formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly places pairwise interactions in the binary knapsack objective and fits the leaf, but it lacks an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Conflict Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants with incompatibility restrictions among selected items.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary knapsack with graph-encoded pairwise incompatibilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a conflict graph whose vertices are the items. The conflict knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i\in V}p_i x_i:\sum_{i\in V}a_i x_i\le B,\ x_i+x_j\le1\ \text{for every }\{i,j\}\in E,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\}.
\]
Consequently, every feasible selected set is an independent set of \(G\) whose total weight does not exceed \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a profitable capacity-feasible subset containing no pair of mutually conflicting items.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph
\(a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{V}\) and \(B\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
\(p\in\mathbb R^{V}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{i\in V:x_i=1\}\) is feasible iff \(S\) is independent in \(G\) and \(\sum_{i\in S}a_i\le B\).

notation.meaning: binary indicator that item i is selected

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-conflict formulation and independent-set characterization are consistent and fit the leaf, but no inspectable supporting source is provided.

children.title: Precedence Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants with prerequisite relations among item selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard 0-1 knapsack model with directed prerequisite relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given items indexed by \(N\), weights \(w_i\ge 0\), profits \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), capacity \(B\ge 0\), and a directed precedence relation \(A\subseteq N\times N\), the precedence knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i\in N}p_i x_i:\sum_{i\in N}w_i x_i\le B,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\ (i\in N),\ x_j\le x_i\ ((i,j)\in A)\right\}.
\]
Thus an arc \((i,j)\) means that selecting item \(j\) requires selecting item \(i\). If \(A\) is acyclic, feasible selected sets are predecessor-closed subsets of the resulting directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a capacity-feasible predecessor-closed set of items maximizing total profit; every selected item requires all predecessors specified by the precedence arcs.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is finite.
\(w_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible vectors are exactly the binary vectors satisfying the capacity and precedence inequalities.

notation.meaning: indicator that item i is selected

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, arc convention, and acyclic predecessor-closed interpretation are mathematically coherent and fit the leaf, but no citation is supplied. An inspectable authoritative locator is required to confirm the intended precedence convention and standard formulation.

children.title: Item-Interaction Boundary
children.top_down_role: The separation between independent-item knapsack structure and relational item structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Item-Interaction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between additive knapsack data and genuine pairwise item interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An item-relation knapsack instance lies on the additive side of the interaction boundary when its objective and feasibility conditions can be written using only individual-item terms, such as \(\sum_i p_i x_i\) and \(\sum_i w_i x_i\le B\). A nonzero pair term or pair restriction crosses the boundary. For example,
\[
f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2
\]
cannot equal \(c+p_1x_1+p_2x_2\) on \(\{0,1\}^2\): its mixed discrete difference is \(1\), whereas every additive function has mixed discrete difference \(0\). Hence the interaction cannot be absorbed into independent item profits without auxiliary structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent item coefficients suffice exactly on the additive side; a nonzero mixed effect, such as a pair bonus, requires an interaction model or auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: Decision variables are binary.
Representation is required to agree on every vector in \(\{0,1\}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair bonus \(x_1x_2\) has no representation as \(c+p_1x_1+p_2x_2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Boolean-function example correctly separates the pair term from affine additive functions on the full Boolean square, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. However, the broader assertion that any pair term or restriction crosses the boundary depends on the permitted feasible domain and auxiliary representation; no source establishes the taxonomy-specific boundary.

children.title: Knapsack Reduction-Representation Interface
children.top_down_role: Reductions and representations that expose dominance, state spaces, relaxations, and decomposable structure.

children.title: Knapsack Preprocessing System
children.top_down_role: Safe simplification families used before exact or approximate solution.

children.title: Dominance Strength Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Classical item-elimination families.

children.title: Simple Dominance
children.top_down_role: Item elimination based on a direct comparison between individual item types.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-wise dominance of one knapsack item by one other item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a maximization knapsack instance, item \(j\) simply dominates a distinct item \(i\) when
\[
w_j\le w_i\quad\text{and}\quad p_j\ge p_i,
\]
with at least one strict inequality if strict dominance is intended. Whenever a feasible selection contains \(i\), excludes \(j\), and permits their exchange, replacing \(i\) by \(j\) does not increase total weight and does not decrease total profit. Availability, precedence, conflict, and multiplicity restrictions must therefore be checked separately before using this parameter test as a deletion rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Item j simply dominates item i when j is no heavier and no less profitable; deletion additionally requires the exchange to respect all side constraints.
assumptions_latex: The objective is profit maximization.
Item weights and profits enter additively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An admissible exchange of \(i\) for \(j\) weakly improves the weight-profit pair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parameter comparison is a coherent condition and the record appropriately distinguishes it from an unconditional deletion rule. A source is still required to verify that this is the intended knapsack definition of simple dominance and to delimit the availability assumptions under which preprocessing deletion is valid.

children.title: Multiple Dominance
children.top_down_role: Item elimination based on comparison with repeated copies of another item type.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance of one item by several available copies of another item type.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In bounded knapsack, item type \(j\) multiply dominates item type \(i\) if there is an integer \(m\) satisfying \(1\le m\le u_j\) such that
\[
mw_j\le w_i\quad\text{and}\quad mp_j\ge p_i.
\]
The predicate says that \(m\) copies of \(j\) weakly improve the weight-profit pair of one copy of \(i\). Applying it to a feasible solution is valid only when those \(m\) copies remain available and the replacement respects every additional constraint. The case \(m=1\) recovers simple dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Item type j multiply dominates i when an available number of copies of j weighs no more and earns no less than one copy of i.
assumptions_latex: Multiplicities satisfy \(0\le x_k\le u_k\).
Weights and profits are additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The replacement bundle \(m e_j\) weakly dominates the single item \(e_i\) in weight and profit.

notation.meaning: upper multiplicity bound for item type j
one unit of item type i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed bundle comparison is mathematically coherent and condition is an appropriate content kind, but multiple dominance has variant-specific definitions in knapsack preprocessing. The global bound m <= u_j does not itself establish residual availability in a solution, so an authoritative source is needed to fix the intended convention.

children.title: Collective Dominance
children.top_down_role: Item elimination based on comparison with a collection of alternative items.

knowledge_statements.title: Collective Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance of one item by a bounded bundle of other item types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In bounded knapsack, a bundle \(y\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{N\setminus\{i\}}\) collectively dominates item type \(i\) when
\[
0\le y_j\le u_j,\qquad \sum_{j\ne i}w_jy_j\le w_i,
\qquad \sum_{j\ne i}p_jy_j\ge p_i.
\]
Thus the bundle weakly improves the weight-profit pair of one copy of \(i\). A preprocessing deletion based on this predicate is sound only if the required bundle is simultaneously available whenever the deleted copy would be used and all additional relations remain satisfied. A bundle supported on one item type gives multiple dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A collection of other item copies collectively dominates item i when its total weight is no greater and its total profit is no smaller.
assumptions_latex: Multiplicities are integral and bounded by \(u_j\).
Weights and profits are additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bundle \(y\) weakly dominates \(e_i\) in the two criteria of weight and profit.

notation.meaning: available multiplicity bound for type j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bundle comparison fits the collective-dominance leaf and is correctly presented as a condition rather than an unconditional deletion theorem. Its precise terminology and the simultaneous-availability requirements for a sound preprocessing rule are source-dependent and currently unsupported.

children.title: Dominance Strength Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: The progression from pairwise comparisons to multiplicity-based or collective comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Strength Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment hierarchy among item, repeated-item, and bundle dominance tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the local dominance predicates, every simple-dominance witness is a multiple-dominance witness with \(m=1\), and every multiple-dominance witness is a collective-dominance witness supported on one item type. Consequently,
\[
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{simple}}\subseteq
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{multiple}}\subseteq
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{collective}}.
\]
The reverse containments need not hold: repeated copies can dominate when no single copy does, and a heterogeneous bundle can dominate when no bundle supported on one type does. This hierarchy compares detection predicates, not unconditional deletion rules; deletion still requires a valid exchange under availability and side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple dominance is a special case of multiple dominance, which is a special case of collective dominance; stronger tests can detect strictly more replacement witnesses.
assumptions_latex: The three predicates use the same additive weight-profit data.
Multiplicity-one and single-support bundles are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{simple}}\subseteq\mathcal D_{\mathrm{multiple}}\subseteq\mathcal D_{\mathrm{collective}}\).

notation.meaning: ordered item pairs certified by dominance test t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The containments follow from the three locally stated predicates, and property fits the hierarchy leaf. Because those predicate conventions remain unsourced, the claimed named hierarchy and its asserted potentially strict reverse containments also require authoritative support.

children.title: Multiplicity-Encoding Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Transformations between bounded and binary representations.

children.title: Multiplicity Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Decompositions that replace bounded item multiplicities with smaller selectable groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact replacement of one bounded integer multiplicity by weighted binary choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be an integer variable with \(0\le x\le u\). Choose positive integers \(q_1,\ldots,q_t\) such that
\[
\left\{\sum_{r=1}^{t}q_r z_r:z\in\{0,1\}^{t}\right\}=\{0,1,\ldots,u\}.
\]
Then the substitution \(x=\sum_{r=1}^{t}q_rz_r\) is an exact multiplicity decomposition. In a bounded knapsack term, \(wx\) and \(px\) become \(\sum_r wq_rz_r\) and \(\sum_r pq_rz_r\), respectively. Thus every original multiplicity has a binary representation and every binary vector maps to an allowed multiplicity, although representations need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded multiplicity is replaced exactly by weighted binary variables whose subset sums are precisely all integers from zero through the upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\).
All decomposition coefficients \(q_r\) are positive integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution preserves exactly the attainable multiplicities and their additive weight and profit contributions.

notation.meaning: multiplicity represented by binary variable r
binary selection variable for block r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset-sum equality gives a precise exact representation and representation is the correct content kind. No source is provided for this bounded-knapsack decomposition convention or its preservation claim, so it cannot yet enter candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Binary Expansion
children.top_down_role: Binary encodings used to represent bounded item counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-of-two decomposition, with one residual block for an arbitrary upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\ge 1\), let \(k=\lfloor\log_2(u+1)\rfloor\) and \(r=u-(2^k-1)\). Use coefficients
\[
1,2,\ldots,2^{k-1}
\]
and, when \(r>0\), one additional coefficient \(r\). Their subset sums cover every integer in \(\{0,1,\ldots,u\}\), and no subset sum exceeds \(u\). Hence a bounded variable can be represented as
\[
x=\sum_{h=0}^{k-1}2^h z_h+r z_k,
\]
where the final term is omitted when \(r=0\). The construction uses \(\lceil\log_2(u+1)\rceil\) binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Powers of two plus one residual block represent every multiplicity up to an arbitrary bound using logarithmically many binary variables.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) is a positive integer.
All variables \(z_h\) are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed expansion represents exactly \(\{0,1,\ldots,u\}\) using \(\lceil\log_2(u+1)\rceil\) binaries.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The powers-of-two-plus-residual construction is mathematically consistent, including the stated binary-variable count, and representation fits the leaf. An inspectable source locator is required for this exact truncated binary expansion rather than a generic reference to binary encoding.

children.title: Encoding-Size Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: The representational balance between variable count and recoverable multiplicities.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Size Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-count and coefficient-size comparison for unary and binary multiplicity encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Encoding a bound \(0\le x_i\le u_i\) by \(u_i\) unit-copy binaries uses \(\Theta(u_i)\) variables and keeps each copied weight and profit equal to \(w_i\) and \(p_i\). Binary multiplicity decomposition uses
\[
\left\lceil\log_2(u_i+1)\right\rceil
\]
binary variables, but creates scaled coefficients as large as \(2^{\lfloor\log_2 u_i\rfloor}w_i\) and \(2^{\lfloor\log_2 u_i\rfloor}p_i\). Thus binary expansion is polynomial in the bit length of \(u_i\), whereas unit-copy expansion is polynomial only in its numeric value and may be pseudopolynomial in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary copies preserve small coefficients but use linear space in the bound; binary decomposition uses logarithmically many variables at the cost of larger coefficients.
assumptions_latex: Bounds and coefficients are encoded in binary.
Encoding size counts binary variables and coefficient bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unary expansion uses \(\Theta(u_i)\) variables, while binary expansion uses \(\Theta(\log(u_i+1))\) variables.

notation.meaning: multiplicity upper bound for item type i

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity_bound is suitable for this leaf, and the unary-versus-logarithmic variable-count comparison is standard. The cited generic encoding page has not been shown to support the exact knapsack comparison. Moreover, the claimed largest scaled coefficient is not explicitly tied to the preceding residual-block construction and should be checked against the chosen encoding before the statement is accepted.

children.title: Residual-Bound Reduction Family
children.top_down_role: Reduction families based on residual feasibility and bounding information.

children.title: Capacity Reductions
children.top_down_role: Preprocessing based on tightening or replacing residual capacity information.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-capacity preprocessing after some items have been fixed as selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a 0-1 knapsack instance and a set \(F\) of items fixed to one, first test \(\sum_{i\in F}w_i\le B\). If it fails, declare the fixing infeasible. Otherwise set
\[
B'=B-\sum_{i\in F}w_i
\]
and remove every unfixed item \(j\) with \(w_j>B'\), fixing its variable to zero. Solve the residual instance on the remaining items with capacity \(B'\), then restore \(x_i=1\) for \(i\in F\). The original objective is recovered by adding the fixed-profit offset \(\sum_{i\in F}p_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract weights of forced selected items from capacity and discard every remaining item exceeding that residual capacity; retain the fixed profit as an objective offset.
assumptions_latex: Variables are binary.
Every item in \(F\) is required to be selected.
Weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual solutions correspond bijectively to feasible original solutions respecting \(x_i=1\) for \(i\in F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-capacity procedure is correct for the stated additive 0-1 knapsack setting and algorithm fits the reduction leaf. No source is supplied, and the claimed bijection implicitly excludes additional item relations unless their residual effects are also handled; an authoritative locator must establish the intended scope.

children.title: Profit Reductions
children.top_down_role: Preprocessing based on objective bounds or profit-value restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Profit Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual target-profit preprocessing for the decision form of knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the decision question whether a 0-1 knapsack solution has profit at least \(P\). For items \(F\) fixed to one, define the fixed-profit offset \(p(F)=\sum_{i\in F}p_i\) and residual target
\[
P'=P-p(F).
\]
After applying the corresponding residual-capacity reduction, ask whether the remaining items can attain profit at least \(P'\). If \(P'\le 0\), the profit requirement is already met and only residual feasibility remains. If a valid upper bound on residual profit is smaller than \(P'\), declare the fixing infeasible for the decision target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract profits of forced selected items from the decision target, then compare the residual target with feasibility and a valid residual-profit upper bound.
assumptions_latex: Profits enter additively.
Every item in \(F\) is fixed as selected.
The residual-profit bound is valid for all residual feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original target \(P\) is attainable under the fixing exactly when residual profit at least \(P'\) is attainable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-target equivalence is coherent for the decision version with additive profits, and algorithm is a plausible role for the leaf. The title could also denote other profit-reduction procedures, so a source is required to establish that this is the intended variant and to support the residual-bound test.

children.title: Variable-Fixing Reductions
children.top_down_role: Preprocessing that fixes item decisions using feasibility or bounding information.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Fixing Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe binary-variable fixing from incumbent and conditional objective bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be the value of a feasible incumbent for a maximization knapsack problem. For each unfixed binary variable \(x_i\), compute valid upper bounds \(U_i^0\) and \(U_i^1\) on the best objective attainable subject to \(x_i=0\) and \(x_i=1\), respectively. Apply
\[
U_i^0<L\ \Longrightarrow\ x_i=1,
\qquad
U_i^1<L\ \Longrightarrow\ x_i=0.
\]
If both inequalities hold, the bounds or incumbent are inconsistent. After any fixing, update residual capacity, profit offsets, and conditional bounds; stop when no new fixing is certified or the residual instance is resolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable value is eliminated when a valid upper bound for that branch is below the incumbent; repeat after updating residual data and bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is attained by a feasible solution.
Each \(U_i^b\) is a valid upper bound conditional on \(x_i=b\).
The problem is a maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any branch with \(U_i^b<L\) contains no optimal solution, so the opposite binary value may be fixed safely.

notation.meaning: conditional objective upper bound for x_i=b

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-bound implications are mathematically sound when preserving at least one optimal solution is the goal, and algorithm fits the preprocessing leaf. An authoritative source is required for this bound-based fixing rule, its strict inequality convention, and the iterative update conditions.

children.title: Residual-Bound Interaction
children.top_down_role: The interaction between residual feasibility, objective bounds, plus decision fixing.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Bound Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe incumbent-bound reduction for a residual 0–1 knapsack subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a partial solution with profit \(p\), residual capacity \(r\), incumbent value \(L\), and a valid upper bound \(U(r)\) on the additional profit attainable by any completion. If \(p+U(r)\le L\), the partial solution and all its descendants may be discarded. Capacity, profit, or variable-fixing reductions may decrease \(r\), remove completion choices, or strengthen \(U(r)\); after each such reduction the bound must be recomputed or remain valid for the reduced completion set. Any reduction yielding \(p+U(r)\le L\) therefore triggers safe pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual subproblem is safely pruned when its current profit plus a valid completion bound cannot exceed the incumbent; preprocessing can strengthen this test.
assumptions_latex: \(U(r)\) upper-bounds every feasible completion profit at residual capacity \(r\).
\(L\) is the value of a feasible incumbent solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p+U(r)\le L\Longrightarrow\) no completion improves the incumbent.

notation.meaning: upper bound on residual completion profit

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy structural characterization of an optimum fractional-knapsack solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let c_1,\ldots,c_n,w_1,\ldots,w_n,W\in\mathbb Z_+ satisfy \sum_{i=1}^n w_i>W, let \{i:w_i=0\}=\{1,\ldots,h\}, and suppose \frac{c_{h+1}}{w_{h+1}}\ge\cdots\ge\frac{c_n}{w_n}. Define k=\min\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\sum_{i=1}^j w_i>W\}. Then the fractional-knapsack instance has an optimum solution given by x_j=1 for j<k, x_k=(W-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}w_j)/w_k, and x_j=0 for j>k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integral profits, weights, and capacity, place all zero-weight items first and order the positive-weight items by nonincreasing profit-to-weight ratio. Fill every item preceding the first capacity-crossing item, take exactly the capacity-filling fraction of that item, and reject all later items; this solution is optimal for fractional knapsack.
assumptions_latex: c_i,w_i,W\in\mathbb Z_+
\sum_{i=1}^n w_i>W
\frac{c_{h+1}}{w_{h+1}}\ge\cdots\ge\frac{c_n}{w_n}
k=\min\{j:\sum_{i=1}^j w_i>W\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_j=\begin{cases}1,&j<k,\\ \dfrac{W-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}w_i}{w_k},&j=k,\\0,&j>k\end{cases}\quad\text{is optimal.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded integer knapsack, efficiency, and sensible solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical single-constraint nonnegative-integer knapsack formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max\{\sum_{i=1}^m c_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^m a_i x_i\le b,\ x_i\in\mathbb Z_+\}\), with \(a_i>0\) and, after deleting variables with \(c_i\le0\), \(c_i>0\). The efficiency of \(x_i\) is \(c_i/a_i\), and variables may be relabeled so that \(c_1/a_1\ge\cdots\ge c_m/a_m\). Every optimal solution then satisfies \(b-\sum_i a_i x_i<a_m\); a feasible solution satisfying this inequality is called sensible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unbounded integer knapsack maximizes total value under one capacity constraint and nonnegative integer multiplicities. Items may be ordered by value-to-size efficiency. With positive sizes and profits, every optimum leaves less residual capacity than the size of the least-efficient item; feasible solutions with this property are called sensible.
assumptions_latex: a_i>0,\quad b>0
x_i\in\mathbb Z_+
c_i>0\text{ after variables with }c_i\le0\text{ are deleted}
\frac{c_1}{a_1}\ge\frac{c_2}{a_2}\ge\cdots\ge\frac{c_m}{a_m}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ optimal}\implies b-\sum_{i=1}^m a_i x_i^*<a_m.

children.title: Compact Integer Models
children.top_down_role: Direct discrete formulations using item-selection variables and compact constraint systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Integer Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard compact binary formulation of 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For items \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with weights \(w_i\ge 0\), profits \(p_i\), and capacity \(B\ge 0\), the 0–1 knapsack problem has the compact integer representation
\[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le B,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.\]
The binary value \(x_i=1\) means that item \(i\) is selected. The model uses \(n\) variables and one nontrivial packing inequality, aside from the integrality restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables select items, one weighted inequality enforces capacity, and the linear objective maximizes total profit.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), \(w_i\ge0\), and \(B\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible binary vectors are exactly \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^\top x\le B\}\).

notation.meaning: weight and profit of item i

children.title: Compact Linear Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Continuous counterparts of compact selection formulations used for bounds or structural comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Linear Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous relaxation of the compact binary knapsack formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), items \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with weights \(w_i\ge 0\) and profits \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and capacity \(B\ge 0\), the standard compact linear relaxation of 0–1 knapsack is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le B,\ 0\le x_i\le1\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.\]
It is obtained from the compact integer model by replacing each restriction \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(0\le x_i\le1\). Every feasible binary solution is feasible for this linear program. Consequently, if \(z_{IP}\) and \(z_{LP}\) are respectively the integer and relaxation optima, then \(z_{IP}\le z_{LP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified 0–1 knapsack instance, allowing each selection variable to range continuously from zero to one gives a compact linear relaxation whose optimum upper-bounds the integer optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), \(w_i\ge0\), \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(B\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^\top x\le B\}\subseteq\{x\in[0,1]^n:w^\top x\le B\}\) and \(z_{IP}\le z_{LP}\).

notation.meaning: weight and profit of item i

children.title: Integrality-Gap Perspective
children.top_down_role: The structural separation between compact discrete models and their continuous relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Perspective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case gap of the standard compact 0–1 knapsack relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(p_i>0\), \(0<w_i\le B\), and a nonempty item set. For the standard compact relaxation, let \(z_{IP}\) and \(z_{LP}\) denote the integer and fractional optima. Then \(z_{IP}>0\) and
\[1\le \frac{z_{LP}}{z_{IP}}<2.\]
The constant \(2\) is the supremum: there are families of instances for which \(z_{LP}/z_{IP}\) approaches \(2\). Thus the compact relaxation supplies a constant-factor upper bound but does not describe the knapsack polytope exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every positive-profit item individually fits, the fractional optimum is less than twice the integer optimum, and ratios can approach two.
assumptions_latex: \(p_i>0\) for every item.
\(0<w_i\le B\) for every item.
The item set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\le z_{LP}/z_{IP}<2\), with \(\sup z_{LP}/z_{IP}=2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical fractional-knapsack bound obtained from the integral prefix and one fractional item
