children.title: Acyclic State-Space Networks
children.top_down_role: Layered capacity- or value-state representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic State-Space Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered capacity-state network for 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral weights and capacity, form vertices \((i,q)\) with \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(q\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\). From \((i-1,q)\), add a skip arc to \((i,q)\) of value \(0\), and, when \(q+w_i\le B\), a take arc to \((i,q+w_i)\) of value \(p_i\). Arcs advance the layer, so the network is acyclic. Source-to-layer-\(n\) paths correspond bijectively to feasible item selections, and maximum path value equals the knapsack optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered acyclic network represents skipping or taking each item; feasible paths correspond exactly to feasible knapsack selections.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\text{source-to-layer-}n\text{ path value}\}=\max\{p^\top x:w^\top x\le B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: state after processing i items with used capacity q

children.title: Nondominated-State Representations
children.top_down_role: Sparse state collections retaining only states not dominated by alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondominated-State Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance-minimal state set for profit-maximizing knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
After processing items \(1,\ldots,i\), let \(S_i\) be the set of attainable pairs \((q,v)\), where \(q\) is total weight and \(v\) is total profit. A state \((q,v)\in S_i\) is dominated if another state \((q',v')\in S_i\) satisfies \(q'\le q\) and \(v'\ge v\), with at least one strict inequality. The nondominated-state representation is
\[N_i=\{(q,v)\in S_i:\text{ no state in }S_i\text{ dominates }(q,v)\}.\]
Discarding dominated states preserves the best attainable profit under every capacity limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is retained exactly when no attainable state uses no more weight and earns no less profit, with one strict improvement.
assumptions_latex: States compared in \(S_i\) use the same processed-item prefix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_i\) contains exactly the states maximal for profit and minimal for weight under the dominance order.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance definition is precise and fits the nondominated-state container, but no source supports the knapsack-specific state representation and preservation claim.

exists(q',v')\in S	ext{ with }q'\le q,\ v'\ge v,\ (q',v')
e(q,v)\}.\]
For every capacity \(B\ge0\) such that \(S\cap([0,B]	imes\mathbb{R})
e\varnothing\), maximizing profit over \(S\cap([0,B]	imes\mathbb{R})\) gives the same value as maximizing over \(\mathcal{F}(S)\cap([0,B]	imes\mathbb{R})\).

children.title: State-to-Frontier Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The relationship between nondominated state sets and their frontier interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: State-to-Frontier Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between nondominated dynamic-programming states and Pareto outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_i\) be the attainable weight-profit states after processing the first \(i\) items. Equip \(S_i\) with the order in which \((q',v')\) dominates \((q,v)\) exactly when \(q'\le q\), \(v'\ge v\), and the pairs differ. Then the nondominated state set and the Pareto frontier coincide:
\[N_i=\mathcal{F}(S_i).\]
Consequently, deleting dominated dynamic-programming states is precisely the operation of replacing the attainable state set by its weight-profit Pareto frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the lower-weight, higher-profit order, nondominated dynamic-programming states are exactly the attainable Pareto-frontier outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(S_i\) contains all attainable weight-profit pairs for the same item prefix.
Both representations use the lower-weight, higher-profit dominance order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_i=\mathcal{F}(S_i)\).

notation.meaning: Pareto frontier of the state set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Profit-indexed dynamic programming algorithm for 0-1 knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dynamic programming indexed by attainable profit, with predecessor indicators for reconstructing an optimal subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given n,c_1,\ldots,c_n,w_1,\ldots,w_n,W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0} and an integer upper bound C on the optimal value, let x(j,k) be the minimum weight of a subset of \{1,\ldots,j\} having value k, with infeasible states assigned \infty. Initialize x(0,0)=0 and x(0,k)=\infty for 1\le k\le C. For j=1,\ldots,n and 0\le k\le C, set x(j,k)=\min\{x(j-1,k),x(j-1,k-c_j)+w_j\}, omitting the second term when k<c_j and treating weights exceeding W as infeasible. Record which transition is chosen. Let k^*:=\max\{k\in\{0,\ldots,C\}:x(n,k)<\infty\}; backtracking through the recorded transitions returns a set S with \sum_{j\in S}w_j\le W and \sum_{j\in S}c_j=k^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each item prefix and profit up to an upper bound C, store the least weight needed to attain that profit. Update each state by excluding or including the next item, discard states exceeding capacity, choose the largest reachable final profit, and backtrack the recorded choices to return an optimal feasible subset.
assumptions_latex: n,c_1,\ldots,c_n,w_1,\ldots,w_n,W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
C\ge\operatorname{OPT}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \sum_{j\in S}w_j\le W,\quad \sum_{j\in S}c_j=\operatorname{OPT}.

children.title: Capacity-Indexed Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Indexed Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial 0–1 knapsack recurrence indexed by capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integral \(B\ge0\) and weights \(w_i\ge0\), define \(D_0(b)=0\) for \(b=0,\ldots,B\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), update
\[D_i(b)=\begin{cases}D_{i-1}(b),&b<w_i,\\ \max\{D_{i-1}(b),D_{i-1}(b-w_i)+p_i\},&b\ge w_i.\end{cases}\]
Here \(D_i(b)\) is the maximum profit attainable from the first \(i\) items with capacity at most \(b\). Output \(D_n(B)\); predecessor choices recover an optimal selection. The table requires \(O(nB)\) arithmetic comparisons and \(O(B)\) working memory when rows are rolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A table indexed by item prefix and capacity compares skipping each item with taking it; the final entry is the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(B,w_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\).
Each item may be selected at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(D_n(B)=\max\{p^\top x:w^\top x\le B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\) in \(O(nB)\) time.

notation.meaning: best prefix profit within capacity b

children.title: Profit-Indexed Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Profit-Indexed Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial 0–1 knapsack recurrence indexed by total profit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume integer profits and set \(P=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\). Initialize \(W_0(0)=0\) and \(W_0(v)=+\infty\) for \(v=1,\ldots,P\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), update
\[W_i(v)=\min\{W_{i-1}(v),\ W_{i-1}(v-p_i)+w_i\},\]
where terms with \(v-p_i<0\) are omitted. The value \(W_i(v)\) is the minimum weight attaining profit exactly \(v\) from the first \(i\) items. Output the largest \(v\) satisfying \(W_n(v)\le B\). The running time is \(O(nP)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A profit-indexed table stores the least weight attaining each profit; the largest profit whose weight fits is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(p_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) and \(w_i\ge0\).
Each item may be selected at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is \(\max\{v:W_n(v)\le B\}\), equal to the 0–1 knapsack optimum, using \(O(nP)\) updates.

notation.meaning: minimum weight attaining exact profit v from the first i items

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Profit-Indexed Dynamic Programming for Zero-One Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact profit-indexed dynamic program, shortest-path interpretation, recovery rule, and numerical running-time bound for zero-one knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\max\{\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j:\sum_{j=1}^n w_jx_j\le K,\ x_j\in\{0,1\}\}\), let \(W_i(u)\) be the minimum weight of a subset of \(\{1,\ldots,i\}\) having total value exactly \(u\), and set \(W_i(u)=\infty\) when no such subset exists. With \(W_0(0)=0\) and \(W_0(u)=\infty\) for \(u\ne0\), \[W_{i+1}(u)=\min\{W_i(u),W_i(u-c_{i+1})+w_{i+1}\}.\] Equivalently, \(W_i(u)\) is the shortest-path weight from state \((0,0)\) to state \((i,u)\) in the inclusion-exclusion transition graph. If \(c_{\max}=\max_j c_j\), it suffices to consider \(0\le u\le nc_{\max}\), giving running time \(O(n^2c_{\max})\). The optimal value is \(u^*=\max\{u:W_n(u)\le K\}\), and an optimal selection is recovered from an optimal transition path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each item prefix and exact attainable profit, store the least weight needed to realize that profit. Update the table by taking the better of excluding or including the next item. This is also a shortest-path computation on the state-transition graph. Profits above n times the largest item profit are unreachable, yielding an O(n squared times the largest profit) algorithm. The largest final profit requiring at most the capacity is optimal, and backtracking recovers a selection.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
K,c_j,w_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
x_j\in\{0,1\}\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
u\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}
c_{\max}=\max_{1\le j\le n}c_j
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u^*=\max\{u:W_n(u)\le K\}\text{ is optimal, an optimal selection is recoverable, and the table is computable in }O(n^2c_{\max})\text{ time.}

knowledge_statements.title: Nemhauser-Ullmann Algorithm Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: List-merging dynamic programming with weight-profit dominance pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(L_0=\{(0,0)\}\). For item \(i=1,\ldots,n\), form the shifted list
\[L_{i-1}^{+i}=\{(q+w_i,v+p_i):(q,v)\in L_{i-1},\ q+w_i\le B\},\]
merge it with \(L_{i-1}\), and delete duplicate or dominated pairs, obtaining
\[L_i=\operatorname{ND}(L_{i-1}\cup L_{i-1}^{+i}).\]
Lists may be maintained in increasing weight order, retaining only strictly increasing profits. After the final merge, output a pair of maximum profit in \(L_n\), with stored predecessors if an item set is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly merge the current state list with an item-shifted copy and discard dominated weight-profit pairs; the final maximum-profit label is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\ge0\), \(B\ge0\), and each item is used at most once.
Dominance means no greater weight and no smaller profit, with one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{v:(q,v)\in L_n\}\) equals the 0–1 knapsack optimum.

notation.meaning: nondominated labels after processing i items

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothed bound on the number of Pareto-optimal subsets relevant to the Nemhauser–Ullmann method.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact knapsack dynamic programming by merging and dominance-pruning Pareto lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonnegative integers \(n,c_1,\ldots,c_n,w_1,\ldots,w_n,W\), initialize \(\mathcal P_0=\{\varnothing\}\). For \(j=1,\ldots,n\), merge the sorted lists \(\mathcal P_{j-1}\) and \(\mathcal P_{j-1}^{+}=\{S\cup\{j\}:S\in\mathcal P_{j-1}\}\), discarding dominated subsets to obtain the sorted Pareto list \(\mathcal P_j\). knowledge_statements.title: Label-Setting Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permanent-label processing on an acyclic knapsack state network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a layered acyclic knapsack network, assign the source label \(0\) and all other state labels \(-\infty\). Process states in a topological order. When state \(u\) is processed, relax every outgoing arc \((u,v)\) of profit \(c_{uv}\) by setting
\[\ell(v)\leftarrow\max\{\ell(v),\ell(u)+c_{uv}\}.\]
If several labels encode resource-profit pairs at a state, discard a label only when another feasible label dominates it. Because every predecessor of a processed state has already been processed, its surviving labels are permanent. Stop after the terminal layer and output its maximum feasible label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process an acyclic state network topologically, relax outgoing arcs, and permanently discard dominated labels; the best terminal label gives the optimum.
assumptions_latex: The state network is finite and acyclic.
Arc transitions preserve feasibility and encode their profit contribution.
Dominance deletion is valid for every remaining continuation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum surviving terminal label equals the maximum value of a feasible source-to-terminal path.

notation.meaning: best value label at state v
profit contribution of arc from u to v

knowledge_statements.title: Label-Dominance Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension compatibility underlying safe label deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(w_a,p_a)\) and \(b=(w_b,p_b)\) be labels at the same dynamic-programming stage, with \(w_a\le w_b\) and \(p_a\ge p_b\). For every common continuation having added weight \(u\ge0\) and profit \(q\), feasibility of \(b+(u,q)\) implies feasibility of \(a+(u,q)\), while \(p_a+q\ge p_b+q\). Hence deleting \(b\) cannot remove every representation of an optimal completion; equality in both coordinates permits retaining either label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lighter and at least equally profitable label remains no worse after any common continuation, so the dominated label can be deleted safely.
assumptions_latex: Both labels have the same set of admissible remaining items.
Feasibility is determined by the additive weight bound \(w\le C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Multiplicity State Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary grouping reduces bounded knapsack to 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each type \(i\) with multiplicity bound \(b_i\), repeatedly choose \(q_{ij}=\min\{2^{j},r\}\), replace the remaining count \(r\) by \(r-q_{ij}\), and create a 0–1 bundle of weight \(q_{ij}w_i\) and profit \(q_{ij}p_i\), starting with \(r=b_i\) and \(j=0\). Every integer count in \(\{0,\ldots,b_i\}\) is representable by a subset of these bundles. Solving the resulting 0–1 instance therefore preserves feasibility and optimal value and uses at most \(\sum_i\lceil\log_2(b_i+1)\rceil\) bundles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split each bounded item type into binary-sized bundles. Every permitted copy count is representable, yielding an equivalent, smaller 0–1 knapsack instance.
assumptions_latex: \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{bounded}}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{bundled\ 0\text{-}1}}\).

copy count represented by one binary bundle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive lexicographic permutation search for a minimum-length open path through planar points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $n\ge 3$ planar points $p_1,\ldots,p_n$, initialize the identity permutation as the incumbent and systematically generate all remaining permutations by advancing each position to the least unused larger index and backtracking when none exists. Whenever a complete permutation $\pi$ is obtained, replace the incumbent $\pi^*$ if $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}d(p_{\pi(i)},p_{\pi(i+1)})<\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}d(p_{\pi^*(i)},p_{\pi^*(i+1)})$. After enumeration, output $\pi^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting with the identity ordering, enumerate all permutations of the planar points using successor and backtracking steps, retain every strictly improving complete ordering, and output an ordering of minimum open-path length.

\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2
\operatorname{cost}(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}d(p_{\pi(i)},p_{\pi(i+1)})

knowledge_statements.title: Horowitz-Sahni Meet-in-the-Middle Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-list exact enumeration for 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the \(n\) items into sets \(A\) and \(B\) of sizes differing by at most one. Enumerate every subset label \((w(S),p(S))\) in each half, discard infeasible and dominated labels from the \(B\)-list, and sort the survivors by weight with prefix-maximum profit. For each feasible \(A\)-label, find the maximum-profit \(B\)-label whose weight is at most \(C-w(S)\); return the best combined pair. The method is exact, uses \(O(2^{n/2})\) space, and runs in \(O(n2^{n/2})\) time under comparison-based sorting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the items, enumerate both subset lists, Pareto-prune one list, and combine each left subset with its best capacity-compatible right subset.
assumptions_latex: The instance is a profit-maximizing 0–1 knapsack with additive weights and profits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(S_A)+p(S_B)=\operatorname{OPT}\) for the returned compatible pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Space-Efficient Meet-in-the-Middle Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-list implicit enumeration reduces meet-in-the-middle storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the items are divided into four blocks of size at most \(\lceil n/4\rceil\), each block has at most \(2^{\lceil n/4\rceil}\) subset labels. Sorted pairwise sums of two block lists can be generated implicitly by heap merging rather than materialized. Streaming the two complementary pair-sum families in compatible weight order permits exact capacity matching while storing only block lists and heap frontiers. This four-list meet-in-the-middle organization uses \(O^*(2^{n/4})\) space and \(O^*(2^{n/2})\) time, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four-way splitting and heap-generated pair sums retain meet-in-the-middle time while reducing storage from roughly square-root to fourth-root exponential size.
assumptions_latex: The computation model permits sorted implicit generation of additive subset labels.
Polynomial factors are suppressed by \(O^*(\cdot)\).
review_flags: Exact applicability and implementation details for profit-weight knapsack require a specialized source.
The stated bounds follow the Schroeppel–Shamir-style four-list paradigm.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Bound Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-bound using the fractional knapsack relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order undecided items by nonincreasing density \(p_i/w_i\). At a search node with profit \(P\), used weight \(W\), and residual capacity \(R=C-W\), greedily pack remaining items fractionally until the first item that does not fit, taking the fitting fraction of that item. Let the resulting value be \(U\). Prune the node when \(U\le L\), where \(L\) is the incumbent feasible profit; otherwise branch on an unfixed item and repeat. When no live node remains, return the incumbent. Because \(U\) is an LP-relaxation upper bound, the returned solution is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the density-ordered fractional knapsack value as an upper bound, pruning any search node unable to beat the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i>0\), \(p_i\ge0\), and decisions satisfy \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\operatorname{OPT}\) when the live-node set becomes empty.

notation.meaning: fractional-relaxation upper bound at a node

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fractional knapsack supplies the canonical valid upper bound for 0–1 knapsack branch-and-bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic cutting-plane scheme for integer knapsack formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an integer feasible set \(X=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax\le b\}\), initialize a polyhedral relaxation \(P_0\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(X)\). At iteration \(t\), optimize the linear objective over \(P_t\). If the optimizer \(x^t\) lies in \(X\), return it. Otherwise, obtain a valid inequality \(a_t^\top x\le\beta_t\) satisfied by every point of \(X\) but violated by \(x^t\), and set \(P_{t+1}=P_t\cap\{x:a_t^\top x\le\beta_t\}\). Any integral optimizer returned by this procedure is optimal for the original integer program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve a relaxation and add valid inequalities separating fractional optimizers. An integral relaxation optimizer is an optimal integer solution.
assumptions_latex: Each added inequality is valid for every point of \(X\).
Each relaxation is optimized exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^t\in X\Longrightarrow x^t\in\arg\max\{c^\top x:x\in X\}\).

Let \(K=\{x\in\{0,1\}^N:\sum_{j\in N}a_jx_j\le b\}\), and let \(C\subseteq N\) satisfy \(\sum_{j\in C}a_j>b\). Define \(E(C)=C\cup\{j\in N\setminus C:a_j\ge\max_{i\in C}a_i\}\). Then the extended cover inequality is
\[
\sum_{j\in E(C)}x_j\le |C|-1.
\]
It is valid for every \(x\in K\): selecting \(|C|\) items from \(E(C)\) has total weight at least \(\sum_{j\in C}a_j>b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cover inequality remains valid after adding every outside item whose weight is at least the cover's largest weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Cover Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extended-cover formula and content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied. The final validity argument is proof text and should be removed when the record is resubmitted with an authoritative source.

children.title: Cover-Strengthening Routes
children.top_down_role: The distinction between coefficient-based lifting and support-based extension.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a cover for a binary knapsack set \(K\).
Each strengthening step is required to preserve validity over \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extension enlarges the unit-coefficient support, whereas lifting assigns validity-preserving coefficients to variables outside the current support.

notation.meaning: A strengthened valid inequality after extension or lifting.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distinction between cover extension and coefficient lifting
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the two classical routes without asserting that either always dominates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Starting from \(\sum_{j\in C}x_j\le |C|-1\), extension identifies variables outside \(C\) that may receive coefficient \(1\) simultaneously by a direct weight argument. Lifting instead computes coefficients \(\alpha_j\), possibly sequentially and order-dependently, such that
\[
\sum_{j\in C}x_j+\sum_{j\notin C}\alpha_jx_j\le |C|-1
\]
remains valid for \(K\). Extension is therefore a support-enlargement rule with prescribed unit coefficients, while lifting is a validity-preserving coefficient-optimization rule. Neither description alone implies universal dominance between all resulting inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover inequalities are strengthened either by extending their unit-coefficient support or by lifting outside variables with computed valid coefficients.
knowledge_statements.title: Cover-Strengthening Routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly distinguishes unit-coefficient extension from coefficient lifting and does not claim universal dominance. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Structured Knapsack Inequality Family
children.top_down_role: Additional structured knapsack-polytope families.

children.title: Configuration Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Knapsack-polytope inequalities derived from structured item configurations.

assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x\in\{0,1\}^N:\sum_{j\in N}a_jx_j\le b\}\).
\(T=Q\cup\{t\}\subseteq N\), \(|Q|=r\), and \(1\le k\le r\).
For every \(S\subseteq Q\) with \(|S|=k\), \(S\cup\{t\}\) is a minimal cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((r-k+1)x_t+\sum_{j\in Q}x_j\le r\) is valid for \(K\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical (1,k)-configuration inequality for a binary knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the classical \((1,k)\)-configuration convention; terminology varies across sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(T=Q\cup\{t\}\) is a \((1,k)\)-configuration when \(|Q|=r\), \(1\le k\le r\), and every set \(S\cup\{t\}\) with \(S\subseteq Q\) and \(|S|=k\) is a minimal cover for \(K\). Its configuration inequality is
\[
(r-k+1)x_t+\sum_{j\in Q}x_j\le r.
\]
Indeed, when \(x_t=0\) the inequality permits all \(r\) companion items, while when \(x_t=1\) it permits at most \(k-1\) of them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distinguished item that forms a minimal cover with every k-subset of r companion items yields the classical configuration inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality follows the stated (1,k)-configuration convention, but that convention and formula require a specific source because terminology varies. The record is a validity property or theorem-like condition-to-inequality statement rather than a bare condition, and the final explanatory sentence is proof text.

children.title: Weight Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Knapsack-polytope inequalities organized through weighted item structures.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^N\) is a nonempty binary knapsack set.
\(w\in\mathbb{R}^N\) is a prescribed item-weight vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta_K(w)\) is valid for \(K\), and its tight right-hand side is \(\beta_K(w)\).

notation.meaning: Support value of the knapsack set in direction w.

review_flags: terminology_ambiguous: weight inequality has multiple specialized meanings in knapsack-polytope literature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the universally valid support-function sense pending identification of the intended specialized family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty binary knapsack set \(K\) and a prescribed coefficient vector \(w\in\mathbb{R}^N\), define
\[
\beta_K(w)=\max\{w^{\mathsf T}y:y\in K\}.
\]
The associated tight weight inequality is
\[
w^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta_K(w).
\]
It is valid for every \(x\in K\), and no smaller right-hand side is valid with the same coefficient vector. A specialized knapsack weight-inequality family requires additional restrictions on \(w\); the supplied context does not determine those restrictions uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any chosen item-weight vector defines a tight valid inequality whose right-hand side is its maximum over feasible knapsack selections.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the generic support-function inequality for an arbitrary set and coefficient vector, not an identified knapsack-polytope family of weight inequalities. The record itself acknowledges that the defining restrictions of the intended family are absent, so it does not fill the immutable terminal container.

children.title: Structured-Inequality Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparative coverage of configuration-based and weight-based strengthening.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq[0,1]^N\) is a common relaxation.
\(H_1=\{x:\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\}\) and \(H_2=\{x:\gamma^{\mathsf T}x\le\delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first inequality dominates the second relative to \(P\) exactly when \(P\cap H_1\subseteq H_2\).

notation.meaning: Halfspaces induced by the two inequalities.
Maximum violation of the second inequality after imposing the first.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxation-relative dominance criterion for valid inequalities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an exact dominance test rather than asserting universal dominance between structured families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For two valid inequalities \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) and \(\gamma^{\mathsf T}x\le\delta\), comparison must be relative to a common relaxation \(P\). The first dominates the second precisely when
\[
P\cap\{x:\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\}\subseteq\{x:\gamma^{\mathsf T}x\le\delta\}.
\]
Equivalently, dominance holds when
\[
\max\{\gamma^{\mathsf T}x-

delta:x\in P,\ \alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\}\le0.
\]
Absent this inclusion, configuration and weight inequalities can only be compared instance by instance through violation, separation strength, or the relaxation bounds they induce.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One structured inequality dominates another only if imposing it on the common relaxation automatically enforces the other inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Inequality Comparison

children.title: Penalization-Aggregation Relaxation Pair
children.top_down_role: Resource penalization and aggregation for generalized variants.

children.title: Lagrangian Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations using penalties for selected resource restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, and the maximization problem has constraints \(Ax\le b\).
\(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\le L(\lambda)\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\), hence \(z^*\le\inf_{\lambda\ge0}L(\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: Lagrangian relaxation value at multiplier lambda.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Lagrangian relaxation for a maximization problem
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization form with complicating inequalities dualized by nonnegative multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
z^*=\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ Ax\le b\},
\]
the Lagrangian relaxation associated with \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) removes \(Ax\le b\) and uses
\[
L(\lambda)=\sup_{x\in X}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\lambda^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\}.
\]
Every originally feasible \(x\) receives a nonnegative penalty adjustment, so \(z^*\le L(\lambda)\). The best Lagrangian upper bound is \(\inf_{\lambda\ge0}L(\lambda)\), provided the displayed supremum and infimum are interpreted in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lagrangian relaxation removes complicating constraints, penalizes their violation through nonnegative multipliers, and minimizes the resulting upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximization-form Lagrangian definition, multiplier sign, and upper-bound direction are consistent with the leaf. A specific authoritative citation is absent, and the sentence deriving the bound from feasible points is proof text.

children.title: Surrogate Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations using weighted aggregation of multiple resource restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, and the maximization problem has constraints \(Ax\le b\).
\(u\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\le S(u)\), where \(S(u)=\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ u^{\mathsf T}Ax\le u^{\mathsf T}b\}\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses one nonnegative aggregation of the complicating inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
z^*=\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ Ax\le b\},
\]
a surrogate relaxation chooses \(u\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\setminus\{0\}\) and replaces all rows of \(Ax\le b\) by their single nonnegative aggregation
\[
u^{\mathsf T}Ax\le u^{\mathsf T}b.
\]
Its value is
\[
S(u)=\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ u^{\mathsf T}Ax\le u^{\mathsf T}b\}.
\]
Every original feasible point satisfies the aggregate constraint, so \(z^*\le S(u)\) for this maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surrogate relaxation replaces several inequalities by one nonnegative weighted aggregate, producing an upper bound for maximization.
knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonnegative single-row aggregation is the standard surrogate relaxation and the definition kind fits. A specific source is required, and the final sentence supplies a validity argument that should not appear as proof text.

children.title: Penalization-versus-Aggregation
children.top_down_role: The distinction between relaxing restrictions through penalties and replacing them through aggregation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, and \(u\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\setminus\{0\}\).
The Lagrangian and surrogate relaxations use the same constraints \(Ax\le b\) and multiplier \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\le S(u)\le L(u)\).

notation.symbol_latex: \(S(u)=\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ u^{\mathsf T}Ax\le u^{\mathsf T}b\}\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pointwise comparison under a shared multiplier in maximization form
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise comparison for the same nonnegative multiplier and maximization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Lagrangian relaxation changes the objective and removes \(Ax\le b\), whereas surrogate relaxation retains the objective and imposes \(u^{\mathsf T}Ax\le u^{\mathsf T}b\). For every surrogate-feasible \(x\),
\[
u^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\ge0,
\]
so
\[
c^{\mathsf T}x\le c^{\mathsf T}x+u^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\le L(u).
\]
Taking the supremum over surrogate-feasible points gives
\[
z^*\le S(u)\le L(u).
\]
Thus aggregation is at least as strong as penalization pointwise for the same multiplier under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the same nonnegative multiplier, the surrogate upper bound is no larger than the Lagrangian upper bound in maximization form.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalization-versus-Aggregation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For the same nonnegative multiplier in the stated maximization convention, the comparison z^* <= S(u) <= L(u) is correct and the property kind fits. The record has no citation and includes a multi-step derivation rather than only the reviewed statement.

children.title: Group Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic relaxations used to support bounding or enumeration in knapsack variants.

assumptions_latex: \(A_B\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular and \(A_N,b\) are integral.
The nonnegativity restrictions on basic variables are dropped, while \(x_N\in\mathbb{Z}_+^{|N|}\) is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation is the group equation \(\sum_{j\in N}[A_j]x_j=[b]\) in \(G=\mathbb{Z}^m/A_B\mathbb{Z}^m\).

notation.meaning: Finite quotient group induced by the integer basis.
Coset of an integer vector modulo the basis lattice.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical corner or group relaxation of an integer equality system
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite abelian group relaxation obtained by dropping basic-variable nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(A_Bx_B+A_Nx_N=b\) with integral data and nonsingular \(A_B\). Drop \(x_B\ge0\), retain \(x_B\in\mathbb{Z}^m\) and \(x_N\in\mathbb{Z}_+^{|N|}\), and quotient by the lattice \(A_B\mathbb{Z}^m\). The resulting group relaxation is
\[
\sum_{j\in N}[A_j]x_j=[b]\quad\text{in}\quad G=\mathbb{Z}^m/A_B\mathbb{Z}^m,
\]
where \([v]=v+A_B\mathbb{Z}^m\). Its objective uses the original or reduced costs of the retained variables, according to the underlying integer-program formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping basic-variable nonnegativity converts an integral equality system into a finite quotient-group equation for the nonbasic variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Group Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient-group formulation is standard under the stated integral nonsingular basis assumptions, and the definition kind fits. A specific source is needed to support the precise corner/group-relaxation convention and the statement about objective coefficients.

children.title: Congruence Structure
children.top_down_role: Modular structure underlying arithmetic feasibility restrictions and state organization.

assumptions_latex: \(A_B\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
\(UA_BV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\) is a Smith normal form with unimodular \(U,V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_Nx_N\equiv b\pmod{A_B\mathbb{Z}^m}\) is equivalent to \((UA_Nx_N)_i\equiv(Ub)_i\pmod{d_i}\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: Smith normal form of the basis matrix.
Invariant factors, with each positive factor dividing the next.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Smith-normal-form representation of an integer quotient lattice
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smith-normal-form description of the congruences induced by an integer basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(UA_BV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\) be a Smith normal form, where \(U,V\) are unimodular and \(d_i>0\) with \(d_i\mid d_{i+1}\). Then
\[
\mathbb{Z}^m/A_B\mathbb{Z}^m\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\mathbb{Z}/d_i\mathbb{Z},
\]
and \(|G|=|\det A_B|=\prod_i d_i\). Moreover,
\[
A_Nx_N\equiv b\pmod{A_B\mathbb{Z}^m}
\]
is equivalent to the componentwise congruences
\[
(UA_Nx_N)_i\equiv(Ub)_i\pmod{d_i},\qquad i=1,

\ldots,m.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smith normal form decomposes the basis quotient group and turns its lattice condition into explicit componentwise modular congruences.
knowledge_statements.title: Congruence Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Smith-normal-form decomposition and componentwise congruence representation are internally consistent with the convention UA_BV=D, and the representation kind fits. No inspectable source with a section, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Group-Congruence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The relationship between group-based relaxations and modular feasibility structure.

assumptions_latex: \(A_B\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular, and \(A_N,b\) are integral.
Basic-variable nonnegativity has been dropped, but integrality of \(x_B\) and nonnegative integrality of \(x_N\) remain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Group-feasible \(x_N\) correspond bijectively to relaxed integer solutions through \(x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between the relaxed equality system and its quotient-group congruence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x_N\in\mathbb{Z}_+^{|N|}\), the quotient-group equation
\[
[A_Nx_N]=[b]\quad\text{in}\quad G=

\mathbb{Z}^m/A_B\mathbb{Z}^m
\]
holds exactly when \(b-A_Nx_N\in A_B\mathbb{Z}^m\). This is equivalent to
\[
x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N)\in\mathbb{Z}^m.
\]
Consequently, group-feasible nonbasic vectors are in bijection with integer solutions of \(A_Bx_B+A_Nx_N=b\) after the restriction \(x_B\ge0\) is removed. Reimposing \(x_B\ge0\) selects precisely those group solutions feasible for the original equality formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quotient-group congruence holds exactly when the basic variables reconstructed from the nonbasic vector are integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Congruence Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lattice-membership correspondence is mathematically standard, but it is a representation or property, not a duality. It also lacks a citation and includes the equivalence derivation as proof text.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling-and-dynamic-programming scheme for nonnegative integral 0–1 knapsack instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonnegative integral profits $c_1,\ldots,c_n$, weights $w_1,\ldots,w_n$, capacity $W$, and $\epsilon>0$, compute a factor-$2$ approximate feasible set $S_1$. If $c(S_1)=0$, return $S_1$. Otherwise set $t=\max\{1,\epsilon c(S_1)/n\}$ and $\bar c_j=\lfloor c_j/t\rfloor$. Apply the dynamic-programming knapsack algorithm to the scaled-profit instance with bound $C=2c(S_1)/t$, obtaining $S_2$, and return whichever of $S_1$ and $S_2$ has greater original profit. The returned set $S$ is feasible and satisfies $c(S)\ge (1+\epsilon)^{-1}c(S')$ for every feasible set $S'$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a factor-2 solution, round the profits after scaling them from that solution, solve the scaled knapsack instance by dynamic programming, and return the better solution. The result is feasible and within a factor 1+epsilon of optimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient conditions for an FPTAS from numerical pseudopolynomial solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General transfer theorem for optimization problems with integer numerical data and linear solution costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every instance be \(I=(S,Q)\), where \(Q=\{q_1,\ldots,q_n\}\subset\mathbb Z\), let \(q=\max_i q_i\), and let \(c_I\) be the optimal cost. Suppose there are polynomials \(p_1,p_2,p_3\) such that \(c_I\le p_1(|I|,q)\), \(q\le p_2(|I|,c_I)\), the cost \(c(f,Q)\) of every feasible solution \(f\) is a linear functional of \(q_1,�\ldots,q_n\), and the problem is exactly solvable in time at most \(p_3(|I|,q)\). Then the problem has an FPTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization problem with integer numerical data has an FPTAS if its optimum and largest numerical value polynomially bound one another, every feasible solution's cost is linear in those data, and an exact algorithm runs in time polynomial in the input length and the largest numerical value.

\forall f\text{ feasible},\;c(f,Q)\text{ is linear in }(q_1,\ldots,q_n).
A\text{ is exactly solvable in time at most }p_3(|I|,q)\text{ for a polynomial }p_3.

children.title: Capacity-Scaling Schemes

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Scaling Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria weight scaling for binary-encoded 0–1 knapsack, allowing controlled capacity augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given items with weights \(w_i\ge 0\), profits \(p_i\ge 0\), capacity \(C>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon\le 1\), set \(K=\varepsilon C/n\), \(\widehat w_i=\lfloor w_i/K\rfloor\), and \(\widehat C=\lfloor C/K\rfloor\). Solve exactly the integer knapsack \(\max\{\sum_i p_i x_i:\sum_i\widehat w_i x_i\le\widehat C,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\}\), and output its selected set \(S\). Then \(p(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(C)\) and \(w(S)<C+nK=(1+\varepsilon)C\). Thus scaling reduces the capacity index to \(O(n/\varepsilon)\) while giving a \((1,1+\varepsilon)\) profit-capacity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding weights downward yields an exact scaled dynamic program with optimal profit, while the selected set may exceed the original capacity by at most an ε fraction.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i,p_i\ge 0\) and \(C>0\)
\(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every item
\(0<\varepsilon\le 1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(C)\) and \(w(S)<(1+\varepsilon)C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bicriteria weight-scaling algorithm and its capacity-augmentation calculation are mathematically coherent and fit the algorithm container, but no inspectable source supports this less-standard knapsack scaling variant.

children.title: List-Trimming Schemes

knowledge_statements.title: List-Trimming Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative list trimming for the subset-sum form of 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n>0\), capacity \(C\), and \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), initialize \(L_0=\{0\}\) and set \(\delta=\varepsilon/(2n)\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), form \(M_i=L_{i-1}\cup\{z+a_i:z\in L_{i-1}\}\), delete entries exceeding \(C\), sort, and retain the first entry and thereafter an entry \(z\) only when \(z>(1+\delta)y\), where \(y\) is the last retained entry. Output \(z^*=\max L_n\). If \(Z^*\) is the largest attainable sum not exceeding \(C\), then \(z^*\ge Z^*/(1+\delta)^n\ge Z^*/(1+\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly merge attainable sums and discard multiplicatively close values. The final retained sum is within a factor 1+ε of the largest feasible subset sum.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,C\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(0<\varepsilon\le1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\ge Z^*/(1+\varepsilon)\ge(1-\varepsilon)Z^*\).

notation.meaning: trimmed attainable-sum list after item i

children.title: Scaling-Trimming Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: The contrast between numerical coarsening and frontier-list compression.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Trimming Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative error-state-space tradeoff for multiplicatively trimmed attainable-value lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each of \(n\) merge steps replaces every discarded positive value \(z\) by a retained representative \(y\) satisfying \(y\le z\le(1+\delta)y\), where \(n\ge1\) and \(\delta>0\). Then every exact attainable value after step \(n\) has a retained representative smaller by at most the factor \((1+\delta)^n\). If retained positive values lie in \([1,U]\), their number is at most \(1+\lceil\log_{1+\delta}U\rceil\); consequently, a list that may also contain zero has at most \(2+\lceil\log_{1+\delta}U\rceil\) entries. For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), choosing \(\delta=\Theta(\varepsilon/n)\) gives total multiplicative loss \(1+O(\varepsilon)\) and list size \(O(n\log U/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smaller trimming tolerance improves accuracy but enlarges lists: per-step error compounds as (1+δ)^n, while the number of positive retained values is logarithmic in U divided by δ; a possible zero entry adds one more state.
assumptions_latex: Each discarded positive value has a retained multiplicative representative.
Retained positive values belong to \([1,U]\).
\(n\ge1\), \(\delta>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{loss}\le(1+\delta)^n\) and \(\lvert L_i\rvert\le2+\lceil\log_{1+\delta}U\rceil\) when \(0\in L_i\) is allowed.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative FPTAS Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common approximate-frontier invariant shared by scaled dynamic programs and trimmed Pareto lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For 0–1 knapsack, let \(F_i\) be the exact nondominated weight-profit pairs attainable from the first \(i\) items. An implementation may store a table indexed by scaled profit, a balanced ordered list, or profit buckets. It is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate frontier implementation when, for every \((w,p)\in F_i\), its stored set \(\widetilde F_i\) contains \((\widetilde w,\widetilde p)\) with \(\widetilde w\le w\) and \(\widetilde p\ge p/(1+\varepsilon)\). If this invariant holds at \(i=n\), selecting the largest stored profit with weight at most \(C\) returns a feasible value at least \(\operatorname{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled tables, ordered lists, and buckets implement the same FPTAS interface when they retain a feasible representative for every exact Pareto state.
assumptions_latex: Profits and weights are nonnegative
Stored states correspond to attainable subsets
The approximate-frontier invariant holds after every update
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{\mathrm{out}}\ge\operatorname{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{out}}\le C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Item Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration of all possible high-profit members of an optimal 0–1 knapsack solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P>0\) satisfy \(P\le\operatorname{OPT}<(1+\varepsilon)P\), where \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and define \(L=\{i:p_i>\varepsilon P\}\). Every optimal solution contains fewer than \((1+\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\) items from \(L\). Enumerate every feasible subset \(G\subseteq L\) with \(\lvert G\rvert\le\lceil(1+\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\rceil-1\); for each \(G\), reserve weight \(w(G)\), invoke a residual-completion routine on capacity \(C-w(G)\), and return the most profitable feasible union. One branch enumerates exactly the large-item portion of an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After guessing the optimum’s scale, an optimal solution contains only O(1/ε) high-profit items, so all possible large-item cores can be enumerated.
assumptions_latex: \(P\le\operatorname{OPT}<(1+\varepsilon)P\)
\(p_i,w_i\ge0\)
\(0<\varepsilon\le1\)

children.title: Residual Completion
children.top_down_role: Approximate completion of the capacity remaining after influential items are fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee obtained by completing a correctly guessed large-item core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) be an optimal knapsack solution, let \(G=O\cap L\), and set \(C'=C-w(G)\). Form a residual instance whose eligible items include every item of \(O\setminus G\). If a completion routine returns a feasible residual set \(R\) satisfying \(p(R)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{res}}(G)\) for some \(0\le\alpha\le1\), then \(G\cup R\) is feasible and \(p(G\cup R)\ge p(G)+\alpha p(O\setminus G)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}\). Consequently, an enumerative algorithm containing the correct-core branch inherits the residual routine's approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When enumeration guesses the optimal large-item core and the residual instance retains the optimum's remaining items, any α-approximate residual completion yields an α-approximate solution to the original instance.
assumptions_latex: \(G=O\cap L\) for an optimal solution \(O\).
Every item in \(O\setminus G\) is eligible in the residual instance.
The residual routine returns a feasible \(\alpha\)-approximation, with \(0\le\alpha\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(G\cup R)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}\) and \(w(G\cup R)\le C\).

notation.meaning: optimal profit of the residual instance after fixing G

knowledge_statements.title: Enumerated-Core Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally checkable certificate connecting an enumerated core to a residual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A core-completion certificate is a pair \((G,R)\) of disjoint item sets together with residual capacity \(C'=C-w(G)\). It is valid when \(w(G)\le C\), \(R\) uses only residual-eligible items, and \(w(R)\le C'\). These conditions certify feasibility of \(G\cup R\). If the certificate additionally identifies \(G=O\cap L\) for some optimum \(O\) and provides the bound \(p(R)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{res}}(G)\), it certifies \(p(G\cup R)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}\). Feasibility is directly verifiable; the approximation premises require the enumeration and residual analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface passes a feasible core and residual capacity to completion; disjointness and two weight checks certify that their union is feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(G\cap R=\varnothing\)
Residual eligibility excludes forbidden or already fixed items
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(G\cup R)\le C\), and under the approximation premises, \(p(G\cup R)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}\).

children.title: Large-Item Threshold Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Item Threshold Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core-size and enumeration bounds induced by a relative profit threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\tau<1\) and a scale \(P\) satisfying \(P\le\operatorname{OPT}<\gamma P\) for some \(\gamma\ge1\). Declare item \(i\) large when \(p_i>\tau P\). Any optimal solution contains fewer than \(\gamma/\tau\) large items, because their total profit is below \(\gamma P\). Hence exhaustive enumeration of its large-item portion requires at most \(\sum_{k=0}^{\lceil\gamma/\tau\rceil-1}\binom{n}{k}=n^{O(\gamma/\tau)}\) candidate cores. For fixed \(\tau\) and \(\gamma\), this enumeration is polynomial; choosing \(\tau=\Theta(\varepsilon)\) gives exponent \(O(1/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold τP limits every optimal core to fewer than γ/τ items, producing n^{O(γ/τ)} candidate cores and an O(1/ε) exponent when τ≈ε.
assumptions_latex: \(P\le\operatorname{OPT}<\gamma P\)
\(0<\tau<1\) and \(\gamma\ge1\)
Profits are nonnegative
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert O\cap L\rvert<\gamma/\tau\) and the number of enumerated cores is \(n^{O(\gamma/\tau)}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weak NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak NP-hardness of binary-encoded 0–1 knapsack via SUBSET SUM.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Binary-encoded decision 0–1 knapsack is weakly NP-hard. In particular, a SUBSET SUM instance with positive integers \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) and target \(B\) maps polynomially to the decision-knapsack instance \(w_i=p_i=a_i\), \(C=B\), and required profit \(P=B\); the SUBSET SUM instance is feasible exactly when the resulting knapsack instance has a subset of weight at most \(C\) and profit at least \(P\). Moreover, integer 0–1 knapsack admits an exact algorithm polynomial in \(n\) and the numerical capacity \(C\), so this algorithm is pseudopolynomial under binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary-encoded decision 0–1 knapsack is weakly NP-hard through the direct SUBSET SUM mapping, while its capacity-indexed exact algorithm is pseudopolynomial.
assumptions_latex: SUBSET SUM integers are encoded in binary.
Knapsack items are selectable at most once.
\(w_i=p_i=a_i>0\) and \(C=P=B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{SUBSET\ SUM}\le_p\mathrm{0\text{-}1\ KNAPSACK}\), and decision 0–1 knapsack is weakly NP-hard.

children.title: Pseudopolynomial Solvability
children.top_down_role: Exact solvability measured against numerical magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact capacity-indexed dynamic programming for integer 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integer weights \(w_i\ge0\), profits \(p_i\ge0\), and integer capacity \(C\ge0\), define \(D_i(c)\) as the maximum profit attainable from items \(1,\dots,i\) with total weight at most \(c\). Initialize \(D_0(c)=0\). For \(i\ge1\), set \(D_i(c)=D_{i-1}(c)\) when \(w_i>c\), and otherwise set \(D_i(c)=\max\{D_{i-1}(c),D_{i-1}(c-w_i)+p_i\}\). Then \(D_n(C)=\operatorname{OPT}\). The computation uses \(O(nC)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(C)\) memory with descending in-place capacity updates, and hence is pseudopolynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-indexed dynamic programming solves integer 0–1 knapsack exactly in O(nC) arithmetic operations and O(C) memory, which is pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in the binary input length.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i,p_i,C\) are nonnegative integers.
Each item is used at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_n(C)=\operatorname{OPT}\), with \(O(nC)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(C)\) memory.

notation.meaning: best profit using the first i items at capacity c

children.title: Encoding-Length Boundary
children.top_down_role: The transition between magnitude-sensitive time and input-length complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Length Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why capacity-indexed pseudopolynomial time is not polynomial under binary numerical encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the binary input length of an integer 0–1 knapsack instance. The capacity contributes only \(\lceil\log_2(C+1)\rceil\) bits to \(L\), and instance families may have \(C=2^{\Theta(L)}\). Consequently, the \(O(nC)\) capacity-indexed dynamic program has an exponential-size capacity range on such families and is not polynomial-time in the binary encoding length. Under unary encoding, or under the promise \(C\le\operatorname{poly}(L)\), the same dynamic-programming bound is polynomial. This is the encoding boundary for the capacity-indexed algorithm, not a claim that binary-encoded 0–1 knapsack is polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The O(nC) capacity dynamic program is polynomial for unary or polynomially bounded capacity, but its capacity range can be exponential in binary input length; this distinction concerns that algorithm, not polynomial-time solvability of binary knapsack in general.
assumptions_latex: Numerical inputs are nonnegative integers.
\(L\) denotes total binary input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(O(nC)\) capacity-indexed bound is polynomial when \(C\le\operatorname{poly}(L)\), but may be exponential in \(L\) under unrestricted binary encoding.

children.title: Fixed-Dimension Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Dimension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudopolynomial dynamic programming for multidimensional 0–1 knapsack with fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(d\)-dimensional 0–1 knapsack with integer resource vectors \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d\), profits \(p_i\ge0\), and capacity vector \(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d\). A dynamic program indexed by \(c=(c_1,\dots,c_d)\), where \(0\le c_j\le C_j\), applies the exclude-or-include recurrence for each item. It computes the exact optimum in \(O\!\left(n\prod_{j=1}^d(C_j+1)\right)\) time and \(O\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^d(C_j+1)\right)\) memory. For fixed \(d\), this is pseudopolynomial and becomes polynomial when every capacity is unary encoded or polynomially bounded in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed dimension d, a capacity-vector dynamic program solves multidimensional 0–1 knapsack exactly in time proportional to n times the product of the coordinate capacity ranges.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is fixed.
\(a_i,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d\) and \(p_i\ge0\).
Each item is selectable at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=O\!\left(n\prod_{j=1}^d(C_j+1)\right)\) and \(M=O\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^d(C_j+1)\right)\).

assumptions_latex: The number of constraints \(d\) is encoded as part of the input.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multidimensional 0-1 knapsack when the dimension belongs to the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multidimensional 0-1 knapsack instance with \(n\) items, dimension \(d\), weights \(a_{ij}\), capacities \(B_j\), and profits \(p_i\), the capacity-indexed dynamic program uses at most \[O\!\left(n\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\right)\] time and \[O\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\right)\] states. If \(d\) and the binary-encoded capacities are unrestricted, then \(\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\) need not be polynomial in the binary input length \(L\); hence this bound is pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With variable dimension and binary capacities, the standard multidimensional capacity dynamic program can require exponentially many states in the encoded input size.

children.title: Dimension-Growth Boundary
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by increasing resource dimension.

assumptions_latex: The input is a multidimensional 0-1 knapsack instance with binary-encoded capacities.
The algorithm explicitly indexes every attainable capacity vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Capacity enumeration is polynomial under fixed bounded dimension and polynomially bounded capacities, but this guarantee disappears when either restriction is removed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for explicit capacity-vector dynamic programming, not a universal algorithmic dichotomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The explicit capacity-vector state space has cardinality \[S(B,d)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1).\] If \(d\) is fixed and every \(B_j\leq L^{c}\) for a constant \(c\), then \(S(B,d)\leq L^{cd}\), so enumeration is polynomial in \(L\). If \(d\) is unbounded, even \(B_j=1\) gives \(S(B,d)=2^d\); if \(d=1\) but \(B_1\) may be exponential in \(L\), then \(S(B,1)\) may likewise be exponential. These are the two dimension-growth boundaries of this state representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-vector enumeration is polynomial for fixed dimension and polynomial capacities, but may be exponential when dimension or binary capacity magnitude grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Growth Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind and algorithm-relative scope fit the leaf, but the capacity-vector boundary has no cited source.

children.title: Parameterized Knapsack Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity organized by capacity, item types, solution size, and dimension.

assumptions_latex: Instances are 0-1 knapsack instances, possibly with \(d\) resource constraints.
All numerical data are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A complexity statement is parameterized only after specifying both the parameter tuple and whether its claimed running time is FPT or XP.

notation.meaning: binary input length of instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A framework for stating parameterized regimes; it does not assert a classification for every tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\), a parameterized knapsack regime is specified by a tuple \(\kappa(I)\) drawn from quantities such as capacity \(B\), number of distinct item types \(\tau\), permitted solution cardinality \(k\), and dimension \(d\). The regime is fixed-parameter tractable if some exact algorithm runs in \[f(\kappa(I))\,|I|^{O(1)},\] where the polynomial exponent is independent of \(\kappa(I)\). It belongs to XP if an exact algorithm runs in \[|I|^{g(\kappa(I))}.\] Parameters and encoding conventions are part of the regime and cannot be omitted from its complexity claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameterized knapsack complexity must name the parameter tuple and distinguish fixed-parameter running time from parameter-dependent polynomial exponents.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Knapsack Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes FPT and XP regimes and fits the topic, but no authoritative locator supports the terminology or formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacity-indexed dynamic programming for unbounded integer knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the intended recurrence with feasible transitions made explicit. This restriction is necessary because the extract's convention \(F(v)=0\) for \(v<0\), combined with an unrestricted maximum over all items, can admit an overweight transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max\{\sum_{i=1}^m p_i a_i:\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i\le W,\ a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\}\), where \(W,w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(p_i\ge0\). Let \(w_{\min}=\min_i w_i\), set \(F(v)=0\) for \(0\le v<w_{\min}\), and, for \(v\ge w_{\min}\), compute \[F(v)=\max\!\left(\{0\}\cup\{F(v-w_i)+p_i: w_i\le v\}\right).\] Evaluating states in increasing order through \(v=W\) yields the optimal value \(F(W)\). Recording a maximizing item at each nonzero transition permits recovery of an optimal multiplicity vector by backtracking. The running time is \(O(mW)\) and the value table uses \(O(W)\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive integer weights and capacity and nonnegative item values, compute the best unbounded-knapsack value for every capacity up to W. At a capacity v, consider only items whose weight is at most v and append one such item to an optimal solution for the remaining capacity. The value at W is optimal, maximizing choices recover a solution by backtracking, and the procedure takes O(mW) time and O(W) table space. Excluding overweight transitions is essential if negative-capacity states are assigned value zero.
assumptions_latex: W\in\mathbb Z_{>0}
w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
p_i\ge0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(W)=\max\left\{p^\top a:\ w^\top a\le W,\ a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\right\},\qquad T(W,m)=O(mW),\quad S(W)=O(W).

children.title: Knapsack Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instance regimes that defeat dense-state, dominance, or relaxation-based methods.

children.title: Encoding-Sensitive State-Space Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure of pseudopolynomial methods under large encoded magnitudes.

children.title: Large-Magnitude Instances
children.top_down_role: Instances whose encoded values are large relative to their description length.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Magnitude Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical-magnitude obstruction for capacity-indexed pseudopolynomial algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(n\geq 1\). For each integer \(m\geq 1\), consider a 0-1 knapsack instance with \(n\) items, capacity \(B=2^m\), and item weights and profits bounded by a polynomial in \(m\). Its binary input length is \(L=\Theta(m)\), while a table indexed by every capacity \(b\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\) has \(B+1=2^m+1=2^{\Theta(L)}\) positions. Thus an \(O(nB)\) capacity-indexed running-time bound can be exponential in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed number of items, a capacity of value 2^m has an input encoding of length proportional to m but induces 2^m+1 capacity indices, so an O(nB) dynamic program can take exponential time in the encoded input length.
assumptions_latex: The number of items \(n\geq 1\) is fixed across the witness family.
Weights, profits, and the capacity are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
The dynamic program indexes every integer capacity from \(0\) through \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family has binary input length \(L=\Theta(m)\) and \(B+1=2^{\Theta(L)}\) capacity indices, so an \(O(nB)\) bound can be exponential in \(L\).

children.title: State-Space Growth
children.top_down_role: Expansion of magnitude-indexed dynamic-programming state spaces.

assumptions_latex: The algorithm retains one value for every integer capacity vector.
Capacities are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of indexed states is \(\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1)\), before accounting for item-processing layers or stored transitions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact size of the rectangular state grid used by capacity-vector dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For capacities \(B_1,\ldots,B_d\), the rectangular index set is \[\mathcal S=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\{0,1,\ldots,B_j\}.\] Hence \[|\mathcal S|=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(B_j+1).\] In the uniform case \(B_j=B\), this becomes \((B+1)^d\). Thus state-space growth is exponential in \(d\) for every fixed \(B\geq1\), and it is exponential in \(\log B\) already for \(d=1\) when \(B\) is binary encoded and may be large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full multidimensional capacity table has a product number of states, growing exponentially with dimension or with the bit length of large capacities.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product state count and its growth statements are correct for the explicitly rectangular capacity table, and complexity_bound fits the leaf, but no source is cited.

children.title: Encoding-Sensitive Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where pseudopolynomial tractability ceases to be operationally useful.

assumptions_latex: The stated running time is polynomial in one or more numerical values.
Those numerical values are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A numerical-value polynomial bound does not imply a polynomial-time bound in the bit model unless the relevant magnitudes are polynomially bounded in the input length.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity test for pseudopolynomial knapsack state-space bounds.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm has running time \(T(I)\leq |I|^{c}M(I)^{q}\) for constants \(c,q>0\), where \(M(I)\) is a binary-encoded capacity, weight, or profit magnitude. Since encoding \(M\) uses \(\Theta(\!\log(M+1))\) bits, instances may satisfy \(M(I)=2^{\Theta(L)}\), where \(L=|I|\). On such a family, the displayed bound permits \(T(I)=2^{\Theta(L)}\). The bound becomes polynomial in \(L\) only under an additional promise \(M(I)\leq L^{r}\) for a constant \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A runtime polynomial in numeric capacity can still be exponential in its binary encoding; polynomial bit complexity needs a magnitude bound or another technique.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Sensitive Failure Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Large Nondominated Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Sparse-state failure caused by weak dominance.

assumptions_latex: A partial solution is represented by total weight and total profit.
Dominance means no greater weight and no smaller profit, with at least one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are \(2^n\) pairwise nondominated partial states, so exact Pareto-frontier pruning need not produce a polynomial state set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete exponential frontier for exact weight-profit dominance pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i\in[n]\), let item \(i\) have weight and profit \(w_i=p_i=2^{i-1}\), and set \(B=2^n-1\). Every subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) is feasible and yields \[w(S)=p(S)=\sum_{i\in S}2^{i-1}.\] Distinct subsets have distinct totals. If \(w(S)<w(T)\), then also \(p(S)<p(T)\), so neither state dominates the other under the order requiring weakly smaller weight and weakly larger profit. Therefore all \(2^n\) subset states are nondominated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Items with equal power-of-two weights and profits create 2^n distinct feasible states, none removable by ordinary weight-profit dominance.
knowledge_statements.title: Large Nondominated Frontiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The power-of-two construction correctly yields an exponential nondominated frontier, and counterexample is the appropriate kind, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

children.title: Core-Concentration Search Failure
children.top_down_role: Search regimes without effective critical-item concentration.

children.title: Diffuse Critical Cores
children.top_down_role: Instances lacking a small concentration of difficult critical items.

assumptions_latex: Items are ordered by nonincreasing ratio \(p_i/w_i\).
A core is a contiguous window around the fractional-knapsack break index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed window radius, instances can place indispensable integer decisions outside the window; therefore no uniform constant-radius core captures every optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-relative boundary for fixed windows centered at a fractional relaxation break item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After sorting items by nonincreasing \(p_i/w_i\), let \(b\) be the first item used fractionally by the linear relaxation and let \[C_r=\{i\in[n]:|i-b|\leq r\}.\] Core concentration with radius \(r\) means that some optimal integer solution agrees with the relaxation-induced fixed decisions outside \(C_r\). A diffuse critical-core family is a sequence of instances for which, for every constant \(r\), all optimal integer solutions disagree with those fixed decisions at some index outside \(C_r\). Such a family invalidates constant-radius core restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical core is diffuse when every fixed window around the fractional break misses an item whose decision must change in every integer optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Diffuse Critical Cores

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement defines diffuse-core failure but does not establish the existence asserted by the conclusion. An explicit witness family and a source fixing the algorithm-specific core convention are required.

children.title: Weak Search Bounds
children.top_down_role: Search regimes with insufficiently discriminating node bounds.

assumptions_latex: A maximization search node has incumbent value \(L\) and valid relaxation upper bound \(U\).
The node is pruned by bounds only when \(U\leq L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(U>L\) persists at many nodes, bound-based pruning cannot eliminate them, regardless of the bound's validity.

notation.meaning: valid upper bound at a search node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational condition for weak pruning in exact maximization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a node \(v\) of an exact maximization search, let \(L\) be the value of the best known feasible solution and let \(U(v)\) be a valid upper bound on every completion below \(v\). Bound pruning is justified exactly when \(U(v)\leq L\). For a tolerance \(\delta>0\), call the bound \(\delta\)-weak at \(v\) when \[U(v)-L>\delta.\] If this inequality holds throughout a set of nodes, none of those nodes can be discarded by the incumbent-bound comparison alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper bound is operationally weak when it remains above the incumbent, preventing bound-based pruning even though the bound is valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Search Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition accurately describes failure of incumbent-bound pruning and the condition kind fits, but no authoritative branch-and-bound locator is supplied.

children.title: Core-Concentration Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of effective search reduction when difficulty remains broadly distributed.

assumptions_latex: A core-search method fixes all decisions outside a selected core.
Only assignments within that core are enumerated or optimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If no optimum agrees with the fixed exterior assignment, restricting search to the core excludes every globally optimal solution.

notation.meaning: selected set of free item indices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact logical failure condition for a core-restricted search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be the feasible set, let \(X^*\) be its globally optimal solutions, and let a core method choose \(C\subseteq[n]\) while fixing \(x_i=\bar x_i\) for every \(i\notin C\). Its restricted feasible set is \[X_C=\{x\in X:x_{[n]\setminus C}=\bar x_{[n]\setminus C}\}.\] Core-concentration failure occurs precisely when \[X_C\cap X^*=\varnothing.\] Under this condition, even exhaustive optimization over the variables indexed by \(C\) cannot recover a global optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Core search fails when every global optimum changes at least one decision that the method fixed outside its searched core.
knowledge_statements.title: Core-Concentration Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-intersection condition is mathematically precise and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the algorithm-dependent core-search framework lacks a source.

children.title: Classical Identical-Bin Packing
children.top_down_role: The standard one-dimensional identical-bin family.

children.title: Offline Bin Packing
children.top_down_role: Complete-information packing.

assumptions_latex: All item sizes satisfy \(0<s_i\leq1\).
All item sizes are known before packing begins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the minimum number of unit-capacity bins over all feasible complete assignments.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical one-dimensional offline bin packing with identical unit-capacity bins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given item sizes \(s_1,\ldots,s_n\in(0,1]\), offline bin packing asks for an integer \(m\geq1\) and an assignment \(a:[n]\to[m]\) satisfying \[\sum_{i:a(i)=j}s_i\leq1\qquad\text{for every }j\in[m].\] The objective is \[\operatorname{OPT}(s)=\min\{m:\text{such a feasible assignment exists}\}.\] The word offline means that the complete sequence \((s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) is available when the assignment is computed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Offline bin packing assigns a fully known set of items to the fewest identical unit-capacity bins without exceeding any bin's capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Offline Bin Packing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a correct definition of classical one-dimensional offline bin packing and fits the terminal container, but it has no citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fernández de la Vega–Lueker bin-packing algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grouping, representative-item packing, and small-item completion for offline bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(I=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) and \(\epsilon>0\), set \(\gamma=\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)\) and \(h=\lceil\epsilon\operatorname{SUM}(I)\rceil\). Rearrange \(I\) as \(L,M,R\), where \(M=K_0,y_1,K_1,y_2,\ldots,K_{m-1},y_m\), such that \(x<\gamma\) for \(x\in L\), \(\gamma\le x\le y_1\) for \(x\in K_0\), \(y_i\le x\le y_{i+1}\) for \(x\in K_i\) and \(1\le i<m\), \(y_m\le x\) for \(x\in R\), \(|K_1|=\cdots=|K_{m-1}|=|R|=h-1\), and \(|K_0|\le h-1\). Pack \(R\) in \(|R|\) bins. Form \(Q\) from \(h\) copies of each \(y_i\), find a packing of \(Q\) using at most \((m+1)/2\) more bins than necessary, and transform it into a packing of \(M\). Fill bins of the two packings having at least \(\gamma\) residual capacity with items of \(L\), then pack the remaining items of \(L\) using Next Fit. The combined packing is the output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a bin-packing instance and epsilon greater than zero, the algorithm separates small items, groups the remaining ordered items around representative sizes, packs the largest group separately, packs repeated representatives and replaces them with the grouped items, fills residual capacity with small items, and applies Next Fit to the small items left over.
assumptions_latex: I=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\text{ is a bin-packing instance}
\epsilon>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (k,f)\text{ is the packing of }I\text{ produced by the stated grouping, representative-packing, replacement, filling, and Next-Fit steps}.
