children.title: Martello-Toth Bin-Packing Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: The classical specialized exact family.

assumptions_latex: Items have sizes \(s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_n>0\) and bin capacity \(1\).
A feasible incumbent upper bound \(U\) and a valid lower bound function \(L\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive bound-guided enumeration returns an optimal bin packing.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound on completions of a partial packing \(P\)

review_flags: The title denotes a historical algorithm family rather than one uniquely specified algorithm.
A Martello-Toth source and exact reduction rules are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact branch-and-bound skeleton associated with the classical family; specific Martello-Toth variants require sourcing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U\) from any feasible packing and place items in nonincreasing size order. At a node containing partial packing \(P\), branch by assigning the next item to each distinct feasible existing bin or to one new bin. Apply only reductions known to preserve at least one optimal completion. Prune the node when \(L(P)\ge U\). When all items are placed, replace the incumbent if the completed packing uses fewer than \(U\) bins. Stop after every generated node has been completed or pruned, and output the incumbent. Because every nonpruned canonical placement is enumerated and every pruning bound is valid, the output is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate canonical item placements, apply valid reductions, and prune partial packings whose lower bound cannot improve the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Martello-Toth Bin-Packing Algorithm Family

children.title: Branch-Reduce Search
children.top_down_role: Exact search organized around systematic instance reduction.

assumptions_latex: A search state \(P\) specifies placed items and residual capacities of its open bins.
The bound \(L(P)\) never exceeds the number of bins in an optimal completion of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search returns an optimal packing after all improving branches are exhausted.
review_flags: No exact bin-packing search source locator was supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact depth-first branch-and-reduce template for canonicalized bin-packing states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from the empty packing and a feasible incumbent of value \(U\). Select an unpacked item at each state \(P\), generate one child for every nondominated feasible placement into an open bin and one child opening a new bin, and apply reductions that preserve an optimal completion. Discard a child whenever \(L(P)\ge U\). If no item remains, update \(U\) and store \(P\) when \(P\) uses fewer bins. Continue until the active-node set is empty. The output is the stored incumbent; optimality follows from the stipulated validity of the bound and reductions and from exhaustive generation of all remaining canonical placements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on feasible placements, reduce equivalent states, and prune by a valid completion bound until the best remaining packing is proved optimal.

children.title: Dominance Search
children.top_down_role: Exact search using dominance relations to discard redundant alternatives.

assumptions_latex: States \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same multiset of unpacked items.
Every completion feasible from \(Q\) can be transformed into a completion from \(P\) using no more bins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: State \(Q\) may be deleted without changing the optimal value of the search.

notation.meaning: minimum final bin count attainable from state \(P\)

review_flags: No source locator for bin-packing dominance criteria was supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic dominance condition; implementation-specific residual-capacity tests are not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(P\preceq Q\) when \(P\) and \(Q\) leave the same items unpacked and, for every feasible completion of \(Q\) with final bin count \(k\), there exists a feasible completion of \(P\) with final bin count at most \(k\). Equivalently, this implication yields \(F(P)\le F(Q)\), where \(F\) is the optimal completion value. If the search retains \(P\), then deleting \(Q\) cannot remove every globally optimal completion. A computable dominance test is sound only if it implies this relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One partial packing dominates another when every completion of the latter can be matched no worse from the former; the dominated state is removable.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic dominance condition is sound and the condition kind fits the container. It supplies no implementable bin-packing dominance criterion, however, and no cited locator supports its intended role in the canonicalized search family.

children.title: Canonicalization Reductions
children.top_down_role: Symmetry-aware restrictions that retain representative bin assignments.

assumptions_latex: Bin labels carry no meaning, and equal-sized items are interchangeable.
A partial packing is represented by its unpacked-item multiset and open-bin residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonicalization merges symmetry-equivalent states without changing their feasible completion values.
review_flags: No source locator for canonical bin-packing reductions was supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry reduction by sorting residual capacities and aggregating indistinguishable remaining items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho(P)\) be the nondecreasing list of residual capacities of the open bins in partial packing \(P\), and let \(m(P)\) record the multiplicity of each remaining item size. Define \(\kappa(P)=(\rho(P),m(P))\). If \(\kappa(P)=\kappa(Q)\), then a permutation of bin labels and permutations among equal-sized items map \(P\) to \(Q\). Consequently, their feasible completions correspond bijectively and use the same numbers of additional bins. An exact search may therefore store only one representative for each value of \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort open-bin capacities and aggregate equal remaining items; states with the same canonical key have equivalent completions and need one representative.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonicalization Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the canonicalization container, and the stated key is valid under the assumed state model in which residual capacities retain every opened bin. A source is still required to establish that this is the intended canonical reduction and that no additional state data affect completions.

children.title: Column-Generation Pricing
children.top_down_role: Implicit discovery of configurations within exact tree search.

assumptions_latex: Item type \(i\) has size \(s_i>0\), demand \(b_i\), and dual multiplier \(\pi_i\).
A pattern \(a\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) is feasible when \(\sum_i s_i a_i\le 1\).

notation.meaning: multiplicity vector of a bin pattern

review_flags: No bin-packing column-generation source locator was supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pricing duality for the Gilmore-Gomory covering master with unit pattern costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the covering master \(\min\{\sum_{a\in\mathcal C}x_a:\sum_{a\in\mathcal C}a_i x_a\ge b_i,\ x_a\ge0\}\), the reduced cost of pattern \(a\) is \(\bar c_a=1-\sum_i\pi_i a_i\). Pricing therefore solves \(v=\max\{\sum_i\pi_i a_i:\sum_i s_i a_i\le1,\ a\in\mathbb Z_+^m\}\). If \(v>1\), an optimizer has negative reduced cost and is added to the master. If \(v\le1\), every feasible pattern has nonnegative reduced cost, so the current dual solution is feasible for the full master and certifies LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing is an integer knapsack problem: value above one produces a negative-reduced-cost pattern, while value at most one certifies full-master LP optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Column Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pricing for the unit-cost set-covering master of one-dimensional bin packing with item types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an optimal dual vector \(\pi\ge 0\) for the current restricted master, solve \[v=\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\pi_i a_i:\sum_{i=1}^m s_i a_i\le C,\ a_i\in\mathbb Z_+\right\}.\] A maximizing vector \(a\) defines a feasible pattern with reduced cost \(1-v\). If \(v>1\), append the pattern to \(\mathcal P'\) and reoptimize. If \(v\le 1\), no omitted pattern has negative reduced cost, and the restricted-master value equals the value of the full linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve an integer knapsack problem to find the feasible pattern of greatest dual weight. Add it when that weight exceeds one; otherwise the current restricted master has reached the full linear-relaxation value.
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) item types with sizes \(s_i\in(0,C]\) and demands \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_+\).

The restricted master is \(\min\{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P'}x_p:\sum_{p\in\mathcal P'}a_{ip}x_p\ge b_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ x_p\ge0\}\), where \(\mathcal P'\subseteq\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal P\) contains every capacity-feasible pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A negative-reduced-cost column exists exactly when \(\max\{\sum_{i=1}^m\pi_i a_i:\sum_{i=1}^m s_i a_i\le C,\ a_i\in\mathbb Z_+\}>1\).

children.top_down_role: Exact selection from configurations under covering requirements.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is the finite set of all capacity-feasible patterns.
Each item type \(i\) has integer demand \(b_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set-covering enumeration model is \(\min\{\sum_p x_p:Ax\ge b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal P}\}\).

notation.meaning: Pattern multiplicity matrix with entries a_ip.
Number of bins using pattern p.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard enumerated set-covering formulation for cutting stock and bin packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-pattern integer formulation allowing patterns collectively to overcover item demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\in\mathcal P\), let \(a_{ip}\) be the number of items of type \(i\) placed in pattern \(p\), and let \(x_p\) count uses of that pattern. The enumerated set-covering formulation is \[\min\left\{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}x_p:\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a_{ip}x_p\ge b_i\ \text{for every }i,\ x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\right\}.\] Its objective counts bins, while its inequalities require every demanded item to occur in at least one selected pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate every feasible bin pattern, select integer multiplicities, minimize their total, and require the selected patterns to cover each item demand.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Covering Enumeration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically precise and fits the leaf, but no source with an inspectable formulation locator is cited.

children.title: Set-Partitioning Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Exact selection from configurations under assignment-equality requirements.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is the finite set of all capacity-feasible patterns.
Each item type \(i\) has integer demand \(b_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set-partitioning enumeration model is \(\min\{\sum_p x_p:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal P}\}\).

notation.meaning: Pattern multiplicity matrix with entries a_ip.
Number of bins using pattern p.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard enumerated set-partitioning formulation for bin packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-pattern integer formulation assigning every demanded item exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\in\mathcal P\), let \(a_{ip}\) be the multiplicity of item type \(i\) in pattern \(p\), and let \(x_p\) count uses of that pattern. The enumerated set-partitioning formulation is \[\min\left\{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}x_p:\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a_{ip}x_p=b_i\ \text{for every }i,\ x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\right\}.\] The equalities impose exact assignment: across all selected bins, each type occurs precisely as many times as demanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate every feasible bin pattern and select integer multiplicities so that each item demand is met exactly while minimizing the bin count.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Partitioning Enumeration

children.title: Configuration-Selection Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural differences between covering-based and partitioning-based masters.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Selection Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison for unit-cost, downward-closed one-dimensional bin-packing configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) have one column for every pattern in \(\mathcal P\), and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\). Define the covering models using \(Ax\ge b\) and the partitioning models using \(Ax=b\), with objective \(\min\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}x_p\). Whenever these models are feasible, \[z_{\mathrm{cov}}^{\mathrm I}=z_{\mathrm{part}}^{\mathrm I}\qquad\text{and}\qquad z_{\mathrm{cov}}^{\mathrm{LP}}=z_{\mathrm{part}}^{\mathrm{LP}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every downward-closed unit-cost pattern is available, the covering and partitioning formulations have equal integer optima and equal linear-relaxation optima.
assumptions_latex: The pattern family \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathbb Z_+^m\) is downward closed: if \(a\in\mathcal P\) and \(0\le a'\le a\) componentwise, then \(a'\in\mathcal P\).
Every pattern variable has unit objective cost.
The demand vector satisfies \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\), and the compared models are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The covering and partitioning integer optima coincide, and their linear relaxations have the same optimal value.

notation.meaning: Integer and linear-relaxation optima of the covering model.
Integer and linear-relaxation optima of the partitioning model.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: downward closure permits surplus occurrences to be removed without increasing unit pattern cost

children.title: Compressed-Network Exact Methods

children.title: Arc-Flow Optimization
children.top_down_role: Integer optimization over explicit state-space networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Flow Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer arc-flow representation of a finite one-dimensional bin-packing pattern network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_i\subseteq E\) contain the arcs labeled by item type \(i\). The arc-flow formulation is \[\min z\] subject to \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e=\begin{cases}z,&v=s,\\-z,&v=t,\\0,&v\in V\setminus\{s,t\},\end{cases}\] \[\sum_{e\in E_i}x_e\ge b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad x_e\in\mathbb Z_+\quad(e\in E),\qquad z\in\mathbb Z_+.\] Its integral feasible flows correspond to multisets of represented feasible patterns, and \(z\) is the number of selected patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Send integral flow through a finite acyclic network whose source-to-sink paths encode feasible patterns. Item-labeled arcs meet demands, and the flow value is the number of bins.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite acyclic network with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
Every \(s\)-\(t\) path encodes one capacity-feasible pattern, and every pattern required by the formulation is represented.
For each item type \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), demand \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_+\), and traversing an arc in \(E_i\) inserts one item of type \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum integral source-to-sink flow satisfying the label-demand inequalities equals the minimum number of represented patterns needed to cover the demands.

notation.meaning: Source-to-sink flow value and number of selected bins.
Set of arcs labeled by item type i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integral flows in an acyclic pattern network decompose into represented source-to-sink paths

children.title: Graph Compression
children.top_down_role: Reduction of attainable-load networks through equivalent-state aggregation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an acyclic labeled network whose source-to-sink paths encode patterns.
A surjection \(q:V\to\bar V\) defines the proposed state identifications.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quotient is coverage preserving exactly when it preserves the attainable label-count vectors and their path costs.

notation.meaning: Network obtained by identifying states under q.
Item-label count vector of a path P.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: quotient correctness characterized by preservation of represented path configurations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic correctness condition for quotienting states in a pattern network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct \(\bar G\) by identifying vertices with the same image under \(q\), retaining induced arc labels and costs. The compression is valid precisely when \[\{(\lambda(P),c(P)):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }G\}=\{(\lambda(\bar P),c(\bar P)):\bar P\text{ is a }q(s)\text{-}q(t)\text{ path in }\bar G\}.\] Thus every original pattern-cost pair has a quotient path, and no quotient path introduces a pattern-cost pair absent from the original network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: States may be merged only when the quotient network represents exactly the same item-count and path-cost pairs as the original network.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Compression

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equality of represented label-count and cost pairs is a precise validity condition and the content kind fits, but no arc-flow compression source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: State Dominance
children.top_down_role: Elimination of states dominated by stronger attainable-load states.

knowledge_statements.title: State Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pattern-and-cost dominance criterion for deleting a state from an arc-flow network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a state \(w\), let \(\mathcal R_w\) be the set of configuration-cost pairs represented by source-to-sink paths that pass through \(w\). State \(u\) dominates state \(v\) when every \((a,c)\in\mathcal R_v\) has a witness \((a,c')\in\mathcal R_u\) with \(c'\le c\), where the witnessing path avoids \(v\). Under this condition, deleting \(v\) preserves at least one no-more-expensive representative of every configuration previously represented through \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is removable when every configuration represented through it also has a no-more-expensive path through another state that does not use the removed state.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite acyclic labeled source-to-sink network.
Each source-to-sink path has a well-defined configuration vector and objective cost.
The proposed dominating state \(u\) and dominated state \(v\) belong to the same pattern network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u\) dominates \(v\), deleting \(v\) does not remove the least-cost available representative of any configuration.

notation.meaning: Configuration-cost pairs represented by source-to-sink paths through state w.
Item-label count vector of a represented configuration.
Cost of a represented source-to-sink path.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: state dominance preserves a no-more-expensive representative of each affected configuration

children.title: Coverage-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reduction regimes that retain the configuration coverage needed for exact optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness criterion for reductions of configuration-encoding arc-flow networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a labeled network \(H\), define \[\mathcal R(H)=\{(a,c):H\text{ has a source-to-sink path encoding configuration }a\text{ with cost }c\}.\] A reduction from \(G\) to \(\bar G\) is coverage preserving when \(\mathcal R(G)=\mathcal R(\bar G)\). For every demand vector \(b\), the integer arc-flow models induced by coverage-preserving networks have the same feasible configuration-multiplicity projections, feasibility status, and optimal objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network reduction is coverage preserving when the original and reduced networks represent exactly the same configuration-cost pairs; their induced integer arc-flow models then have the same projected feasible solutions and optima.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(\bar G\) are finite labeled acyclic networks with designated sources and sinks.
Each source-to-sink path represents a configuration and has a well-defined objective cost.
Both arc-flow models impose the same demand vector \(b\) on their represented configurations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality \(\mathcal R(G)=\mathcal R(\bar G)\) implies equality of the induced feasible configuration-multiplicity projections and optimal objective values.

notation.meaning: Configuration-cost pairs represented by network H.
Item-demand vector shared by the compared models.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equal represented configuration-cost sets induce equivalent integer configuration models

children.title: Packing Performance Calculus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines instancewise, absolute worst-case, and large-optimum asymptotic approximation ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an approximation algorithm \(A\) for a minimization problem, define \(R_A(I)=A(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\); for a maximization problem, define \(R_A(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)/A(I)\). Its absolute performance ratio is \(R_A=\inf\{r\ge1: R_A(I)\le r\ \forall I\in D_\Pi\}\). Its asymptotic performance ratio is \(R_A^\infty=\inf\{r\ge1:\exists N\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\ \forall I\in D_\Pi,\ \operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge N\Rightarrow R_A(I)\le r\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The instancewise ratio divides the algorithm value by the optimum for minimization and the optimum by the algorithm value for maximization. The absolute ratio is the least uniform upper bound over all instances. The asymptotic ratio is the least bound that holds for every instance once the optimum is at least some positive-integer threshold.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an approximation algorithm for }\Pi
I\in D_\Pi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite-solution combinatorial optimization problems and distinguishes approximation algorithms from exact optimization algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A combinatorial optimization problem \(\Pi\) is a minimization or maximization problem consisting of an instance set \(D_\Pi\), a finite candidate set \(S_\Pi(I)\) for every \(I\in D_\Pi\), and a value function \(m_\Pi(I,\sigma)\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\). An optimal solution \(\sigma^*\in S_\Pi(I)\) minimizes \(m_\Pi(I,\sigma)\) in the minimization case and maximizes it in the maximization case; its value is \(\operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(I)\). An approximation algorithm \(A\) returns some \(\sigma\in S_\Pi(I)\) for every \(I\in D_\Pi\), with returned value denoted \(A(I)\). It is an optimization algorithm precisely when \(A(I)=\operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(I)\) for every \(I\in D_\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combinatorial optimization problem has a set of instances, a finite candidate-solution set for each instance, and a positive rational solution-value function. An optimum minimizes or maximizes this value as appropriate. An approximation algorithm returns a candidate solution on every instance, and it is an exact optimization algorithm when its value equals the optimum on every instance.
assumptions_latex: \Pi\text{ is a minimization or maximization problem}
\forall I\in D_\Pi,\quad S_\Pi(I)\text{ is finite}
\forall I\in D_\Pi,\ \forall\sigma\in S_\Pi(I),\quad m_\Pi(I,\sigma)\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is exact}\iff \forall I\in D_\Pi,\ A(I)=\operatorname{OPT}_\Pi(I).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-instance multiplicative performance for offline bin-packing algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The absolute approximation ratio of \(A\) is \[R_A=\sup_{I:\,0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty}\frac{A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}.\] Equivalently, \(A\) has absolute ratio at most \(R\) when \(A(I)\le R\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every admissible finite instance \(I\), without an additive constant and without excluding instances having small optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absolute ratio is the worst returned-bin-count divided by optimum over all finite instances, including instances with small optimum.

children.title: Asymptotic Approximation
children.top_down_role: Performance allowing lower-order additive effects.

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is an algorithm for a minimization problem.
Instances have finite positive optimum, which is unbounded over the instance family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic approximation ratio is \(R_A^\infty=\limsup_{k\to\infty}\sup_{\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge k}A(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).

notation.meaning: Objective value returned by algorithm A.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard asymptotic approximation ratio for bin packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case multiplicative performance after lower-order effects vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic approximation ratio of \(A\) is \[R_A^\infty=\limsup_{k\to\infty}\ \sup_{I:\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge k}\frac{A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}.\] Equivalently, \(R_A^\infty\le R\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(K\) such that \(A(I)\le(R+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) whenever \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge K\). A fixed additive constant therefore does not affect this ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic ratio measures worst-case multiplicative performance as optimum grows, so fixed additive losses disappear.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its additive-constant interpretation are mathematically consistent and fit the leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is cited.

children.top_down_role: Adversarial sequential-arrival performance.

assumptions_latex: Items arrive sequentially and irrevocable packing decisions precede future arrivals.
\(A(\sigma)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)\) count bins used on finite sequence \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic competitive ratio is \(R_A^{\mathrm{comp}}=\inf\{R:\exists\beta\ge0\ \forall\sigma,\ A(\sigma)\le R\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta\}\).

notation.meaning: Bin count used online by A on arrival sequence sigma.
Offline optimal bin count for the complete sequence.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard deterministic asymptotic competitive-ratio definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic adversarial competitive analysis with an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a deterministic online algorithm \(A\), its asymptotic competitive ratio is \[R_A^{\mathrm{comp}}=\inf\left\{R\ge1:\exists\beta\ge0\ \text{such that}\ A(\sigma)\le R\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta\ \text{for every finite arrival sequence }\sigma\right\}.\] Here \(A\) must place each arriving item without knowing later items, whereas \(\operatorname{OPT}\) may use the entire sequence. The absolute competitive ratio is obtained by requiring \(\beta=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An online algorithm is asymptotically R-competitive when its bin count never exceeds R times offline optimum plus a sequence-independent constant.

children.title: Partition Reduction Route
children.top_down_role: The arithmetic feasibility route to bin-packing hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Reduction Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak NP-hardness reduction from PARTITION to two-bin feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) satisfy \(a_i\le B\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=2B\). Construct a bin-packing instance with item sizes \(a_i\), bin capacity \(B\), and target two bins. Then the items admit a packing into at most two bins if and only if there exists \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(\sum_{i\in S}a_i=B\). Consequently, the bin-packing decision problem is NP-hard; because the numerical values are inherited from PARTITION, this route establishes weak rather than strong NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition into two equal-sum subsets exists exactly when the corresponding items fit into two bins of that common capacity, yielding weak NP-hardness.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(a_i\le B\) for every \(i\).
\(\sum_i a_i=2B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S:\sum_{i\in S}a_i=B\iff \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{BP}}\le2\).

notation.meaning: bin capacity and half the total item size

children.title: Three-Partition Strong-Hardness Route
children.top_down_role: The strong-hardness route for classical bin packing.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Partition Strong-Hardness Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong NP-hardness reduction using the restricted THREE-PARTITION problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(3m\) positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_{3m}\) and \(B\) satisfy \(B/4<a_i<B/2\) and \(\sum_i a_i=mB\). Form a bin-packing instance with capacities \(B\). It can be packed into \(m\) bins if and only if the integers can be partitioned into \(m\) triples, each summing to \(B\). Indeed, every feasible \(m\)-bin packing has exactly three items per bin under these bounds. Since restricted THREE-PARTITION is strongly NP-complete, classical bin packing is strongly NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted three-partition is feasible exactly when its items fill m capacity-B bins; the size bounds force three items per bin and yield strong NP-hardness.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(a_i,B\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(B/4<a_i<B/2\) for all \(i\).
\(\sum_i a_i=mB\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{BP}}=m\iff\{a_i\}\text{ has a THREE-PARTITION}\).

notation.meaning: number of required triples and target bins

children.title: Approximation Barriers

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute approximation threshold inherited from the two-versus-three-bin gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Unless \(P=NP\), no polynomial-time bin-packing algorithm has an absolute approximation ratio \(\rho<3/2\). For the instances produced by the PARTITION reduction, a yes-instance has optimum \(2\), whereas a no-instance requires at least \(3\) bins. If an algorithm always returned a feasible packing using at most \(\rho\operatorname{OPT}\) bins, then on an optimum-two instance its integral output would be at most \(2\), while every no-instance would require at least \(3\). The algorithm would therefore decide PARTITION in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute ratio below three halves would distinguish two-bin instances from instances requiring at least three bins, so it is impossible unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm runs in time polynomial in the binary input length.
Its guarantee is absolute: \(A(I)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance \(I\).
\(P\ne NP\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho\ge 3/2\) for every polynomial-time absolute-ratio guarantee.

notation.meaning: number of bins returned on instance I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate and the two-versus-three integral gap supports the stated absolute-ratio barrier, but no inspectable source is cited.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative approximation hardness for classical bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Unless \(P=NP\), for every \(\rho<\frac{3}{2}\), there is no \(\rho\)-factor approximation algorithm for the bin-packing problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless P equals NP, bin packing has no rho-factor approximation algorithm for any rho strictly below 3/2.
assumptions_latex: P\ne NP
\rho<\frac{3}{2}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No }\rho\text{-factor approximation algorithm exists for bin packing.}

children.title: Additive-Gap Barriers
children.top_down_role: Hardness limits on guarantees expressed through additive excess.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Gap Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subunit additive error collapses to exact optimization because bin counts are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible packing satisfying \(A(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\delta\) for every bin-packing instance \(I\), where \(0\le\delta<1\). Since both \(A(I)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) are integers and feasibility gives \(A(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), the guarantee forces \(A(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) on every instance. Thus, unless \(P=NP\), no polynomial-time algorithm can provide a uniform additive error strictly below one for classical bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because bin counts are integers, additive error below one means exact optimization, which is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I)\) is the size of a feasible packing.
\(0\le\delta<1\).
\(P\ne NP\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\delta\) for all \(I\) is impossible in polynomial time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integrality argument is precise and failure_boundary fits the additive-gap terminal, but the complexity conclusion depends on the uncited NP-hardness of exact bin packing.

children.title: Guarantee-Regime Boundary
children.top_down_role: The distinction among absolute, asymptotic, and additive performance limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Guarantee-Regime Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between asymptotic approximation schemes and absolute multiplicative guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), classical one-dimensional bin packing admits a polynomial-time asymptotic approximation scheme producing a packing with \(A(I)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)+C_\varepsilon\), where \(C_\varepsilon\) is independent of \(I\). In contrast, unless \(P=NP\), no polynomial-time algorithm can guarantee \(A(I)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for all instances when \(\varepsilon<1/2\). Thus an additive term permits arbitrarily small asymptotic multiplicative loss, while the corresponding absolute guarantee crosses the hardness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bin packing has asymptotic schemes with an additive constant, but an absolute ratio below three halves is impossible unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed independently of the input.
Bin capacities and item sizes are rational and binary encoded.
For the impossibility clause, \(P\ne NP\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{APTAS}\) guarantees exist, but an absolute \((1+\varepsilon)\)-guarantee with \(\varepsilon<1/2\) does not.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement appropriately contrasts asymptotic and absolute guarantee regimes, but both the APTAS existence claim and the absolute-ratio lower bound require authoritative citations with specific locators.

children.title: Bin-Packing Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structures causing poor heuristics, weak formulations, or excessive enumeration.

children.title: Adversarial Arrival Sequences
children.top_down_role: Sequential instances exploiting irrevocability.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Arrival Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indistinguishable-prefix mechanism for lower bounds on deterministic online packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an online bin-packing algorithm assign each arriving item irrevocably before seeing later items. An adversarial pair consists of sequences \(P\mathbin{\|}X\) and \(P\mathbin{\|}Y\) sharing a prefix \(P\), such that every placement state reachable by the algorithm after \(P\) is incompatible with an optimal completion for at least one of \(X\) or \(Y\). An adaptive adversary reveals \(P\), observes the resulting state, and chooses that incompatible continuation. The algorithm must then use more bins than the offline optimum on the selected sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adversary presents a common prefix, observes the irrevocable packing, and chooses a continuation for which that state cannot be completed optimally.
assumptions_latex: Items arrive sequentially and have sizes in \((0,1]\).
Assignments are irrevocable and bin capacity is \(1\).
The online algorithm is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(P\mathbin{\|}Z)>\operatorname{OPT}(P\mathbin{\|}Z)\) for some \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\).

notation.meaning: concatenation of prefix P and continuation Z

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indistinguishable-prefix mechanism fits the terminal and failure_boundary kind, but the existence and quantifier scope of the adversarial pair are not tied to a particular algorithm or lower-bound theorem, and no source is supplied.

children.title: Residual-Capacity Fragmentation
children.top_down_role: Instances with unusable residual-capacity profiles.

assumptions_latex: \(k\ge 2\) and \(0\le r_j\le 1\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
Items are indivisible and each bin has capacity \(1\).
\(\max_{1\le j\le k} r_j<s\le\sum_{j=1}^k r_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The item of size \(s\) requires opening a new bin despite aggregate residual capacity at least \(s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total free capacity may be unusable when dispersed across bins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(k\ge 2\) unit-capacity bins whose residual capacities are \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\). If an arriving item has size \(s\) satisfying \(\max_{1\le j\le k} r_j<s\le\sum_{j=1}^k r_j\), then the aggregate unused capacity is at least \(s\), but the item fits in no existing bin and a new bin is necessary. Hence total residual capacity alone is not a sufficient statistic for extendability: its distribution among bins determines whether subsequent indivisible items can be placed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free space can be sufficient in total yet unusable because no individual bin has enough residual capacity for the next item.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Capacity Fragmentation

children.title: Symmetry-Induced Search Duplication
children.top_down_role: Equivalent bin assignments enlarging compact search trees.

children.title: Bin Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Equivalence created by interchangeable bins.

knowledge_statements.title: Bin Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation invariance of identical bin labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a formulation with \(m\) identical bins, let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate assignment of item \(i\) to bin \(j\), and let \(y_j\) indicate whether bin \(j\) is used. For every permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), replacing \(x_{ij}\) by \(x_{i,\pi(j)}\) and \(y_j\) by \(y_{\pi(j)}\) preserves assignment constraints, capacity constraints, and the objective \(\sum_j y_j\). Thus all label permutations of a packing represent the same unlabeled solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permuting identical bin labels preserves feasibility and objective value, so many labeled solutions represent one packing.
assumptions_latex: All bins have the same capacity and cost.
Constraints contain no bin-specific data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetric group \(S_m\) acts by objective-preserving permutations on feasible labeled packings.

notation.meaning: permutation group on m bin labels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The permutation-invariance property exactly matches Bin Symmetry and property is the correct knowledge kind, but no formulation or integer-programming symmetry source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Search Duplication
children.top_down_role: Repeated exploration of equivalent packing assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Search Duplication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorial multiplicity caused by exploring labeled copies of one packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a feasible unlabeled packing uses exactly \(k\) nonempty identical bins whose item sets are pairwise distinct. In a labeled-bin search with at least \(k\) available labels, assigning these item sets to an ordered selection of labels produces \(m!/(m-k)!\) distinct labeled nodes when \(m\) labels are available, including \(k!\) copies when \(m=k\). Without symmetry detection or canonical branching, a search procedure may explore every such node although all belong to one permutation orbit and have identical objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One unlabeled packing using k distinct bins has k-factorial labeled copies, potentially multiplying equivalent search work factorially.
assumptions_latex: The \(k\) nonempty bin contents are pairwise distinct.
The search distinguishes bin labels.
No symmetry pruning identifies permutation-equivalent states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The labeled multiplicity is \(m!/(m-k)!\), and equals \(k!\) when \(m=k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The falling-factorial orbit count is mathematically consistent under the stated distinct-content assumption, and complexity_bound fits the terminal, but the search-exploration interpretation lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Impact
children.top_down_role: Search-space changes produced by selecting canonical representatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Impact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical bin ordering selects one representative from each permutation orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_j\) denote the load of labeled bin \(j\). Adding the valid symmetry-breaking constraints \(L_1\ge L_2\ge\cdots\ge L_m\), with a fixed lexicographic tie-break on bin contents when loads coincide, preserves at least one representative of every feasible unlabeled packing. It retains exactly one representative whenever the tie-break defines a total order on bin contents. Consequently, the factorial family of label permutations can be reduced to a canonical state without changing the optimal bin count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordering bins by load and breaking ties canonically preserves one representative of every packing while removing label-permutation duplicates.
assumptions_latex: Bins are identical in capacity and cost.
The tie-break totally orders bin-content vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonical ordering preserves the optimum and selects one labeled representative per permutation orbit.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit-representative property fits Symmetry-Breaking Impact, but the fixed lexicographic tie-break is not formally defined as constraints on a specified bin-content representation, and no source supports the validity and uniqueness claim.

children.title: Representation-Growth Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial growth in pattern and network representations.

children.title: Configuration Explosion
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial proliferation of feasible packing patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family of feasible single-bin configurations can be exponentially large.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge1\), consider one item of each type \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with size \(s_i=2^{-(i+1)}\) and unit bin capacity. Since \(\sum_{i=1}^n s_i<1\), every subset of the \(n\) types is a feasible single-bin configuration. Distinct subsets give distinct incidence vectors, so the explicit configuration set has cardinality \(2^n\). Therefore a configuration-based formulation may require exponentially many columns even though the item-type description has only \(n\) entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all item types together fit in one bin, every subset is feasible, producing two-to-the-n distinct configurations.
assumptions_latex: There is one item of each of \(n\) types.
Bin capacity is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of feasible configuration incidence vectors is \(2^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit family correctly has 2^n feasible incidence configurations and complexity_bound fits Configuration Explosion, but no configuration-formulation source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: State-Space Explosion
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial proliferation of attainable-load network states.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-capacity dynamic programs grow exponentially with the number of bins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a dynamic program records the residual capacity of each of \(m\) bins, and each residual belongs to a discrete set of \(q\) levels. With labeled bins there are \(q^m\) possible residual vectors. If bin labels are quotiented out and a state is stored as the multiset of its residual levels, the number of possible profiles is \(\binom{q+m-1}{m}\). Thus symmetry compression reduces the state count but does not make it polynomial when both \(q\) and \(m\) vary with the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual vectors have q-to-the-m labeled states; removing bin labels leaves a binomial number of multisets, still superpolynomial when both parameters grow.
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) bins represented in each state.
Each residual capacity takes one of exactly \(q\) discrete levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{labeled}}=q^m\) and \(N_{\mathrm{unlabeled}}=\binom{q+m-1}{m}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The labeled-vector and unlabeled-multiset counts are correct and complexity_bound fits the terminal. The joint-parameter nonpolynomial conclusion needs a clearly specified input-size regime and an authoritative source.

children.title: Representation-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance structures controlling growth in pattern-based or network-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding turns capacity-indexed bin-packing formulations from polynomial-size numerical schemes into exponential-size representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For item sizes \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and bin capacity \(B\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), a dynamic program or extended formulation indexed by all capacities \(0,\ldots,B\) has \(\Theta(nB)\) states or comparable size. Under unary encoding this is polynomial in the input length. Under binary encoding, the numeric value \(B\) may be exponential in \(\lceil\log_2(B+1)\rceil\); hence a representation polynomial in \(n\) and \(B\) is only pseudo-polynomial and can be exponential in the binary input length. Likewise, explicitly listing every feasible bin configuration can require exponentially many columns in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-indexed models are polynomial under unary encoding but may be exponentially large under binary encoding; explicit feasible-configuration lists can also be exponential.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,B\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(a_i\le B\) for every item \(i\).
Numerical data are compared under unary and binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A size bound polynomial in \(n\) and \(B\) need not be polynomial in the binary input length.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the asserted Θ(nB) state count, the unspecified extended formulation, or exponential configuration growth. The capacity-indexed claim must be tied to a particular formulation or algorithm.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given raw rolls of one or more standard widths and customer demands for specified quantities of narrower final-roll widths, the cutting-stock problem is to select cuts of the raw rolls that fulfill the demands as economically as possible, accounting for unused residual width.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cutting-stock problem seeks an economical plan for cutting standard-width raw rolls into the requested quantities and widths of narrower final rolls, with leftover width constituting waste.

children.title: One-Dimensional Stock-Supply Families
children.top_down_role: Length-based cutting distinguished by the available stock assortment.

children.title: Single-Stock-Size Cutting Stock
children.top_down_role: The classical identical-stock family.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Stock-Size Cutting Stock
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical one-dimensional cutting stock with unlimited identical stock objects and demand covering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let stock objects all have length \(L>0\), let item types have lengths \(\ell_i>0\) and integer demands \(d_i\ge0\), and define the pattern set \(P=\{a\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m:\sum_{i=1}^m \ell_i a_i\le L\}\). The single-stock-size cutting-stock problem chooses integer multiplicities \(x_p\ge0\) for \(p\in P\) to solve \[\min \sum_{p\in P}x_p\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Thus every used stock object has the same length, and each selected pattern describes one feasible cutting of that object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose feasible patterns for identical stock lengths so that every item demand is covered while minimizing the number of stock objects used.
assumptions_latex: \(L,\ell_i>0\), \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\), and \(\ell_i\le L\).
An unlimited supply of stock objects of length \(L\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the minimum number \(\sum_{p\in P}x_p\) of identical stock objects whose patterns cover \(d\).

notation.meaning: number of items of type i in pattern p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical definition fits the container, but it has no citation and repeatedly uses the corrupted notation \(\mathbb Z_{3e0}\) instead of a defined nonnegative-integer domain.

children.title: Stock-Type Cost Family
children.top_down_role: Cutting with several standardized stock types or costs.

children.title: Multiple-Stock-Size Cutting
children.top_down_role: Cutting with several standardized stock dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Stock-Size Cutting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional cutting stock with several available stock lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let stock types be \(k=1,\ldots,q\), with lengths \(L_k>0\), and let item type \(i\) have length \(\ell_i>0\) and demand \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\). For each \(k\), define \(P_k=\{a\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m:\sum_i\ell_i a_i\le L_k\}\). Multiple-stock-size cutting chooses \(x_{kp}\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\) and minimizes a specified stock-use objective, commonly \(\sum_{k,p}x_{kp}\), subject to \[\sum_{k=1}^q\sum_{p\in P_k}a_{ip}x_{kp}\ge d_i\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Each chosen variable uses one stock object of type \(k\) according to a pattern feasible for its length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Patterns may be selected from several stock lengths, with combined production required to cover every item demand.
assumptions_latex: \(L_k,\ell_i>0\) and \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\).
Every demanded item type fits at least one stock type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible solutions are nonnegative integer pattern multiplicities satisfying the aggregate demand-covering inequalities.

notation.meaning: patterns feasible for stock type k
number of type-k stocks cut with pattern p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The family description is plausible, but no source supports it. The nonnegative-integer notation is corrupted, and minimizing the unweighted number of stock objects is only one objective variant for multiple stock sizes.

children.title: Costed-Stock Cutting
children.top_down_role: Cutting where stock use carries type-dependent acquisition costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Costed-Stock Cutting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Configuration formulation in which using each stock type incurs a specified cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stock types \(k=1,\ldots,q\), let \(c_k\ge0\) be the cost of one stock object and let \(P_k\) be its feasible cutting patterns. If item type \(i\) has demand \(d_i\), costed-stock cutting is the integer program \[\min_{x}\ \sum_{k=1}^q c_k\sum_{p\in P_k}x_{kp}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{k=1}^q\sum_{p\in P_k}a_{ip}x_{kp}\ge d_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad x_{kp}\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}.\] Pattern-dependent costs are included by replacing \(c_k\) with coefficients \(c_{kp}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select cutting patterns across stock types to cover demand at minimum total acquisition or usage cost.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_k\) contains precisely the patterns feasible for stock type \(k\).
Costs and demands satisfy \(c_k\ge0\) and \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective equals the total cost of the stock objects assigned selected cutting patterns.

notation.meaning: unit cost of stock type k
multiplicity of pattern p on stock type k
production of item type i by pattern p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied. Because patterns are stock-type-specific, production should be indexed unambiguously as \(a_{ikp}\) or explicitly defined for each \(p\in P_k\); the present \(a_{ip}\) notation can collide across pattern sets.

children.title: Stock-Type Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between stock dimensions, availability, and acquisition cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Stock-Type Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance relation between stock types when both usable length and acquisition cost differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two unlimited stock types \(k\) and \(h\) with lengths \(L_k,L_h\) and nonnegative costs \(c_k,c_h\). If \(L_k\le L_h\) and \(c_k\ge c_h\), then type \(k\) is dominated: every pattern feasible for type \(k\) is feasible for type \(h\), and replacing each use of \(k\) by \(h\) preserves production while weakly decreasing cost. Consequently, some optimal solution uses no type-\(k\) stock. When length and cost move in the same direction, neither type is generally dominated; the preferred type depends on which patterns satisfy demand with less waste and total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A no-shorter, no-costlier stock type dominates another; otherwise length, waste, and cost can create genuine tradeoffs.
assumptions_latex: Both stock types are available without inventory bounds.
Pattern feasibility depends only on total cut length not exceeding stock length.
No type-specific constraint requires use of type \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L_k\le L_h\) and \(c_k\ge c_h\), an optimum exists with \(\sum_{p\in P_k}x_{kp}=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance property is correct under the stated unlimited-supply, length-only feasibility assumptions, but no citation supports it. A source must also confirm the intended model excludes type-specific constraints and stock-dependent pattern effects.

children.title: Heterogeneous-Stock Supply Family
children.top_down_role: Cutting from finite or individually heterogeneous stock.

children.title: Limited-Inventory Cutting
children.top_down_role: Cutting with finite availability for each stock type.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited-Inventory Cutting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heterogeneous cutting stock with an upper bound on available objects of each stock type.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let stock type \(k\) have feasible pattern set \(P_k\), available inventory \(u_k\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\), and pattern-use variables \(x_{kp}\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\). Limited-inventory cutting imposes \[\sum_{p\in P_k}x_{kp}\le u_k\qquad(k=1,\ldots,q)\] together with the production requirements \[\sum_{k=1}^q\sum_{p\in P_k}a_{ip}x_{kp}\ge d_i\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] A feasible solution therefore assigns at most the available number of stock objects of each type while covering demand. The objective may minimize stock cost, waste, or another specified linear pattern cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover item demand using type-specific cutting patterns without exceeding the available inventory of any stock type.
assumptions_latex: \(u_k,d_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\).
Each pattern in \(P_k\) is feasible for one stock object of type \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires both \(Axaw d\) and \(\sum_{p\in P_k}x_{kp}\le u_k\) for every stock type \(k\).

notation.meaning: available inventory of stock type k
patterns feasible for stock type k
multiplicity of pattern p for stock type k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inventory formulation fits the container, but it lacks a source. The conclusion contains the undefined command \raw, and the nonnegative-integer notation is corrupted throughout.

children.title: Residual-Stock Cutting
children.top_down_role: Cutting from previously used or individually sized stock remnants.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Stock Cutting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cutting model that treats heterogeneous residual pieces as explicitly available stock objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite set of residual stock objects, where residual \(s\) has usable length \(R_s>0\). Its feasible patterns are \(P_s=\{a\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m:\sum_i\ell_i a_i\le R_s\}\). Residual-stock cutting selects at most one pattern for each physical residual, using variables \(x_{sp}\in\{0,1\}\), subject to \[\sum_{p\in P_s}x_{sp}\le1\quad(s\in S),\qquad \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{p\in P_s}a_{ip}x_{sp}\ge d_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] New stock variables may be added when residuals alone need not cover demand; the objective specifies their cost and any value assigned to unused remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat each reusable offcut as an individually available stock object and assign at most one feasible pattern to it.
assumptions_latex: Residual lengths \(R_s\) and item lengths \(\ell_i\) are positive.
Each indexed residual is physically available at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each residual receives at most one cutting pattern, and aggregate residual and optional new-stock production covers demand.

notation.meaning: set of available residual stock objects
indicator that residual s receives pattern p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes this residual-stock variant. The displayed model uses residuals only, whereas the conclusion asserts coverage by residuals and optional new stock whose variables and constraints are not defined; the nonnegative-integer notation is also corrupted.

children.title: Stock-Heterogeneity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Supply regimes distinguished by stock identity, dimensions, or remaining quantity.

knowledge_statements.title: Stock-Heterogeneity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified configuration representation for differences in stock length, cost, inventory, and physical identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional heterogeneous-stock instance is represented by stock classes \(k=1,\ldots,q\), parameters \((L_k,c_k,u_k)\), and class-specific pattern sets \(P_k=\{a\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m:\sum_i\ell_i a_i\le L_k\}\). Its common configuration model is \[\min\sum_{k,p}c_{kp}x_{kp}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{k,p}a_{ip}x_{kp}\ge d_i,\qquad \sum_{p\in P_k}x_{kp}\le u_k,\qquad x_{kp}\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}.\] Unlimited supply is represented by \(u_k=+\infty\); identical stock by \(q=1\); and individually tracked residuals by giving each physical piece its own class with \(u_k=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lengths, costs, inventories, and identities fit one configuration model; standard stock regimes arise by specializing class parameters.
assumptions_latex: Stock and item lengths are positive.
Demands and finite inventories are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical, multiple-size, limited-inventory, and residual-stock regimes are specializations of the displayed class-indexed model.

notation.meaning: length, cost, and inventory of stock class k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unified representation is plausible but unsupported. The objective uses undefined \(c_{kp}\) despite introducing \(c_k\), the integer-domain notation is corrupted, and \(u_k=+\infty\) should be formalized as omission of the corresponding finite inventory constraint.

children.title: Cutting Output-Residual Policy Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Variants distinguished by fulfillment, overproduction, and reusable residual material.

children.title: Demand Covering with Overproduction
children.top_down_role: The canonical covering interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Demand Covering with Overproduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical cutting-stock covering model permitting unrestricted surplus production.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a set of feasible cutting patterns, let \(a_{ip}\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\) denote production of item type \(i\) by pattern \(p\), and let \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\) be demand. Demand covering with overproduction requires \[\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\qquad(i=1,26hellip,m),\qquad x_p\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}.\] The surplus of item type \(i\) is \(s_i=\sum_p a_{ip}x_p-d_i\ge0\). Unless the objective penalizes it, no explicit upper bound is imposed on \(s_i\); feasibility depends only on meeting or exceeding demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected cutting patterns must produce at least the demand of each item type, and surplus production is permitted without an explicit upper bound.
assumptions_latex: Pattern outputs and demands are nonnegative integers.
Pattern multiplicities are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pattern vector is feasible exactly when \(Ax\ge d\), with overproduction vector \(s=Ax-d\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The canonical covering definition fits the container, but no source is supplied. The formulas contain corrupted nonnegative-integer notation and the malformed index range \(i=1,26hellip,m\).

children.title: Surplus-Control Cutting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Production variants restricting surplus output.

children.title: Exact-Demand Cutting
children.top_down_role: Production variants requiring exact fulfillment of item demands.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Demand Cutting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surplus-free cutting in which aggregate pattern output must equal every demand exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonnegative integer pattern-output matrix \(A=(a_{ip})\), an integer demand vector \(d\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m\), and nonnegative integer pattern multiplicities \(x\), exact-demand cutting imposes \[Ax=d.\] Equivalently, for every item type \(i\), \(\sum_p a_{ip}x_p=d_i\). Thus neither shortage nor overproduction of any modeled item type is permitted. Waste within a stock object may still occur because a feasible pattern need not exhaust its stock length; exactness concerns produced item counts, not trim loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose feasible cutting patterns whose aggregate item counts equal demand exactly; unused stock length may still remain within patterns.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(d\) have nonnegative integer entries.
Pattern multiplicities satisfy \(x\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^{|P|}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to \(Ax=d\), or surplus vector \(Ax-d=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-demand definition is mathematically standard and matches the container, but it has no citation and uses corrupted notation for nonnegative integer vectors.

children.title: Bounded-Overproduction Cutting
children.top_down_role: Production variants permitting surplus only within specified limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Overproduction Cutting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand covering with an itemwise finite allowance for surplus output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^{m\times |P|}\) be a pattern-output matrix, let \(d\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m\) be demand, and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m\) be the permitted itemwise overproduction. Bounded-overproduction cutting requires \[d\le Ax\le d+b,5cqquad x\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^{|P|},\] where inequalities are componentwise. Equivalently, the surplus vector \(s=Ax-d\) must satisfy \(0\le s\le b\). Setting \(b_i=0\) enforces exact demand for type \(i\), while omitting or making an upper bound infinite recovers unrestricted demand covering for that type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pattern output must cover demand, but each item type may exceed demand by no more than its prescribed allowance.
assumptions_latex: \(A,d,b\) have nonnegative integer entries.
Pattern multiplicities are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to the existence of \(s\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^m\) satisfying \(Ax=d+s\) and \(0\le s\le b\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-surplus formulation fits the container, but it has no source. Its displayed constraint contains the corrupted token 5cqquad, and all nonnegative-integer domains use corrupted notation.

children.title: Surplus-Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Demand policies distinguished by the permitted extent of overproduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Surplus-Control Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified itemwise representation of exact, bounded, unrestricted, and penalized surplus policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For pattern output \(Ax\) and demand \(d\), introduce surplus \(s=Ax-d\). An itemwise surplus-control regime is represented by \[Ax=d+s,5cqquad 0\le s_i\le b_i,5cqquad x\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}^{|P|},\] with extended bounds \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_{3e0}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Exact demand is \(b_i=0\); bounded overproduction is \(0<b_i<+\infty\); and unrestricted covering is \(b_i=+\infty\). Soft control instead retains \(b_i=+\infty\) and adds a nondecreasing surplus penalty \(\phi_i(s_i)\) to the objective. Different item types may use different regimes in the same instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Surplus bounds unify exact, bounded, and unrestricted production, while objective penalties provide soft surplus control.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(d\) are nonnegative integral.
Each hard surplus bound is nonnegative integral or \(+\infty\).
Each soft penalty \(\phi_i\) is defined on \(\mathbb Z_{3e0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choices of \(b_i\) and optional \(\phi_i\) encode the principal hard and soft surplus-control regimes.

notation.meaning: surplus vector equal to output minus demand
hard surplus bound for item type i
soft penalty on surplus of item type i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unifying representation is plausible but unsupported. Its display contains corrupted 5cqquad tokens and corrupted integer-domain notation; the soft-control variant also needs an explicitly defined objective and a source supporting its inclusion in this taxonomy.

children.title: Reusable-Offcut Management System
children.top_down_role: Models retaining offcuts as future stock.

children.title: Usable Leftovers
children.top_down_role: Offcuts retained because they satisfy future usability criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Usable Leftovers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional reusable-offcut criterion relative to admissible future item lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an original stock length be \(L>0\), and let a cutting pattern consume total length \(u\le L\), including required kerf. Its residual length is \(r=L-u\). Given a prescribed usability threshold \(\tau>0\) and a set \(D\subseteq(0,L]\) of admissible future item lengths, the residual is a usable leftover precisely when \(r\ge \tau\) and \(r\ge d\) for at least one \(d\in D\). Equivalently, when \(D\ne\varnothing\), usability is characterized by \(r\ge\max\{\tau,\min D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual is usable when it meets the storage threshold and is long enough to produce at least one admissible future item.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau>0\) and \(D\subseteq(0,L]\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\text{ is usable}\iff r\ge\tau\text{ and }(\exists d\in D)\,r\ge d\).

notation.meaning: residual stock length after cutting and kerf
minimum storable or reusable residual length

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses reusable-offcut usability criteria.
Threshold convention is application-dependent and requires domain-source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but no cited source supports the usability convention. Moreover, an arbitrary nonempty set D need not have a minimum, so the stated equivalent characterization requires an additional assumption such as finite D or existence of min D.

children.title: Remnant Management
children.top_down_role: Inventory treatment of retained residual stock.

knowledge_statements.title: Remnant Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inventory transition rule for storing, consuming, and discarding one-dimensional remnants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a multiset \(R_t\) of available remnant lengths, demands \((d_i)_{i\in I_t}\), a minimum retained length \(\tau>0\), and a feasible cutting plan. Initialize the plan with stock selected from \(R_t\) and optional new stock. Execute every assigned cut, subtracting item lengths and kerf from its selected stock piece. For each resulting residual \(r\), retain one labeled copy in \(R_{t+1}\) if \(r\ge\tau\); otherwise discard it. Remove every remnant consumed during the period. Output the updated multiset \(R_{t+1}\) and the realized cutting plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The procedure allocates old and new stock, performs cuts, removes consumed remnants, and stores only residual pieces meeting the retention threshold.
assumptions_latex: All assigned cuts fit their selected stock pieces after kerf.
Remnants are individually identifiable and their lengths are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{t+1}=(R_t\setminus C_t)\uplus\{r:r\text{ is produced and }r\ge\tau\}\), where \(C_t\) is the multiset of consumed remnants.

notation.meaning: multiset of remnants available at period t
multiset of remnants consumed in period t

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this remnant-inventory transition rule.
Operational conventions for kerf, labeling, and disposal require confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is a suitable kind for the inventory-update procedure, but no source supports the retention, consumption, kerf, labeling, or disposal conventions. These choices materially determine the transition rule.

children.title: Future-Stock Valuation
children.top_down_role: The role of anticipated future utility in remnant retention.

knowledge_statements.title: Future-Stock Valuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic continuation-value model for reusable residual stock.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a finite multiset of retained remnants and let \(\Omega\) be a finite set of future demand scenarios. For scenario \(\omega\in\Omega\), let \(p_\omega\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega=1\), and let \(Q(R,\omega)\) be the minimum future procurement and cutting cost when inventory \(R\) is available. The future-stock value of \(R\), relative to having no remnants, is \(V(R)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega[Q(\varnothing,\omega)-Q(R,\omega)]\). Thus positive value measures expected avoided future cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Future-stock value is the expected reduction in optimal future cost obtained by retaining the remnants instead of beginning with none.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is finite and \((p_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}\) is a probability distribution.
Each recourse value \(Q(R,\omega)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(R)=\mathbb{E}[Q(\varnothing,\omega)-Q(R,\omega)]\).

notation.meaning: optimal future cost under scenario omega and inventory R

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses stochastic valuation of cutting-stock remnants.
The avoided-cost convention is plausible but not uniquely determined by the node title.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and fits future-stock valuation, but the expected avoided-cost convention is only one possible valuation model and has no supporting citation.

children.title: Higher-Dimensional Cutting Boundary
children.top_down_role: Spatial cutting families recorded as neighboring subjects without duplicating their layout theory.
