knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Due dates either require enough cumulative output by each deadline or induce nonnegative tardiness equal to completion beyond the deadline.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\ge0\) and \(a_{ip}\ge0\)
\(u_{vp}\in\{0,1\}\) assigns patterns to executions.
Completed output is available at its completion time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On-time output satisfies the cumulative-demand inequality, or \(T_i\ge\max\{0,C_i-d_i\}\).

notation.meaning: due date and required quantity of item i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and condition role are appropriate, but the cumulative-output expression uses the decision-dependent set v with C_v at most d_i without an explicit linear or logical formulation. Moreover, the tardiness inequalities give only a lower bound unless tardiness is minimized or equality is otherwise enforced.

children.title: Open-Stack Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Coordination of pattern order with open-stack considerations.

knowledge_statements.title: Open-Stack Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence constraints limiting simultaneously unfinished customer or order stacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let execution positions be \(t=1,\ldots,T\), and let \(q_{it}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that order \(i\) has received at least one required item by position \(t\) but still lacks some required item after position \(t\). The number of open stacks after position \(t\) is
\[O_t=\sum_i q_{it}.\]
For a stack-capacity limit \(K\), the cutting sequence is feasible only if \(O_t\le K\) for every \(t\). The indicators \(q_{it}\) are determined by the positions of the first and last pattern executions contributing to order \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every sequence position, the number of orders already started but not yet completed cannot exceed the stack limit.
assumptions_latex: The cutting sequence has positions \(1,\ldots,T\).
\(q_{it}\in\{0,1\}\) exactly identifies started, unfinished orders.
\(K\in\mathbb Z_+\) is the available stack capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i q_{it}\le K\) for every sequence position \(t\).

notation.meaning: indicator that order i is open after position t
number of open stacks after position t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stack-capacity condition matches the open-stack leaf, but no source is cited and the constraints that make q_it exactly represent an order between its first and last contributing executions are not supplied.

children.title: Stock-Sourcing Assortment Interface
children.top_down_role: Coupling to stock purchasing and assortment design.

children.title: Stock Procurement Coupling
children.top_down_role: Links between cutting plans and stock purchasing decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stock Procurement Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Material balance linking purchased stock units to cutting-pattern consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For stock type \(s\) and period \(t\), let \(P_{st}\in\mathbb Z_+\) be purchased units, \(B_{st}\in\mathbb Z_+\) ending stock inventory, and \(x_{pt}\in\mathbb Z_+\) pattern executions. If pattern \(p\) consumes \(b_{sp}\) units of stock type \(s\), procurement and cutting are coupled by
\[B_{s,t-1}+P_{st}=\sum_p b_{sp}x_{pt}+B_{st}\qquad\text{for every }s,t,\]
with \(B_{s0}\) given. Procurement cost \(c_{st}P_{st}\) may therefore be optimized jointly with cutting and stock-holding costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opening stock plus purchases equals stock consumed by cutting patterns plus ending stock in every period.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{st},B_{st},x_{pt}\in\mathbb Z_+\)
\(b_{sp}\in\mathbb Z_+\)
No stock loss or disposal occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{s,t-1}+P_{st}=\sum_p b_{sp}x_{pt}+B_{st}\) for every \(s,t\).

notation.meaning: purchased units of stock type s
ending inventory of stock type s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The procurement material balance is coherent and its representation kind fits the leaf, but it has no inspectable source supporting the stated cutting-procurement interface.

children.title: Stock-Assortment Design
children.top_down_role: Selection of stock sizes or types offered to the cutting system.

knowledge_statements.title: Stock-Assortment Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of stock types made available to the cutting-pattern system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether stock type \(s\) belongs to the designed assortment, and let \(x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\) count pattern \(p\). If \(s(p)\) is the stock type required by pattern \(p\), assortment feasibility is imposed by
\[x_p\le U_p y_{s(p)}\qquad\text{for every }p,\qquad \sum_s y_s\le K,\]
where \(U_p\) is a valid pattern-count bound and \(K\) is the maximum number of offered stock types. Fixed assortment costs may be represented by \(\sum_s f_sy_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting pattern can be used only when its stock type is selected, and the number of selected stock types may be limited.
assumptions_latex: \(y_s\in\{0,1\}\) and \(x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\)
\(U_p\) is a valid upper bound.
\(K\in\mathbb Z_+\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_p\le U_p y_{s(p)}\) for every \(p\), and \(\sum_s y_s\le K\).

notation.meaning: stock type used by pattern p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The activation and assortment-cardinality conditions fit the design leaf, but no cited source supports this particular assortment formulation or its assumptions.

children.title: Purchase-Availability Constraints
children.top_down_role: Procurement limits affecting available stock quantities or types.

knowledge_statements.title: Purchase-Availability Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Period-specific bounds and lead times governing purchasable stock.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_{st}\in\mathbb Z_+\) be the order quantity of stock type \(s\) placed in period \(t\), with availability bound \(A_{st}\ge0\) and lead time \(\ell_s\in\mathbb Z_+\). Purchase feasibility requires
\[0\le P_{st}\le A_{st}\qquad\text{for every }s,t.\]
Only \(P_{s,t-\ell_s}\) may enter the material balance as a receipt in period \(t\); orders with \(t-\ell_s<1\) contribute no receipt unless predetermined pipeline inventory is specified. If a supplier activation variable \(y_{st}\) is used, the upper bound becomes \(P_{st}\le A_{st}y_{st}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orders respect period availability, become usable only after their lead time, and may additionally require supplier activation.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{st}\in\mathbb Z_+\) and \(A_{st}\ge0\)
\(\ell_s\in\mathbb Z_+\)
Pipeline receipts, if any, are specified separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{st}\le A_{st}\), and an order placed at \(t\) is received at \(t+\ell_s\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The availability bound and lead-time interpretation fit the condition leaf, but the receiving-period material balance is only described rather than stated, and no source supports the chosen indexing and pipeline convention.

children.title: Cutting-Stock Failure Boundaries

children.title: Degenerate-Master Convergence Failures
children.top_down_role: Slow column-generation convergence under alternative patterns.

children.title: Restricted-Master Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate behavior within the restricted pattern master.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Master Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duplicate columns exhibit degeneracy and ineffective restricted-master expansions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the restricted master problem
\[\min\ x_1+x_2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2\ge1,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.\]
Its optimal face is \(\{(x_1,x_2):x_1+x_2=1,\ x_1,x_2\ge0\}\), and the dual optimum is \(\pi=1\). Both identical columns have reduced cost \(1-\pi=0\). Consequently, pivots may change the basis or redistribute weight between duplicate patterns without improving the objective. Adding further duplicate zero-reduced-cost patterns enlarges the restricted master but leaves its optimal value unchanged, illustrating the degeneracy boundary behind stalling and unstable dual prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate pattern columns create multiple optimal representations; zero-reduced-cost additions can change the basis without improving the restricted-master objective.
assumptions_latex: The master is solved as a linear program.
Columns have identical covering coefficients and unit costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Duplicate columns have zero reduced cost at \(\pi=1\), and adding them does not change the optimal value \(1\).

notation.meaning: dual multiplier of the covering constraint

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example establishes duplicate columns, alternative optima, and zero reduced costs, but it does not by itself establish primal restricted-master degeneracy in the standard basic-feasible-solution sense. An authoritative column-generation source and a corrected degeneracy example or more precise failure classification are required.

children.title: Pricing Tailing-Off
children.top_down_role: Weak late-stage improvement from newly generated patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Tailing-Off
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic boundary for slow column-generation progress in a minimization master problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_t\) be the optimal restricted-master value after iteration \(t\), let \(z^*\) be the full-master LP value, and let \(\delta_t<0\) be the minimum reduced cost returned by exact pricing. Pricing tailing-off occurs when \(z_t>z^*\) for every finite \(t\), while \(\delta_t\to0\) and \((z_t-z_{t+1})/(z_t-z^*)\to0\). Thus improving columns continue to exist, but their relative effect on the remaining master gap vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tailing-off occurs when negative-reduced-cost columns persist but approach zero value and each iteration closes a vanishing fraction of the remaining LP gap.
assumptions_latex: \(z_t\) is finite and nonincreasing.
Pricing is exact at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\delta_t\to0,\qquad z_t>z^*,\qquad \frac{z_t-z_{t+1}}{z_t-z^*}\to0.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes the standard column-generation diagnosis of vanishing reduced costs and vanishing relative master improvement
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits the failure-boundary leaf, but the proposed asymptotic criterion is a strong, nonstandard formalization of tailing-off and lacks evidence establishing its hypotheses and scope.

children.title: Alternative-Pattern Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of interchangeable patterns contributing to slow progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-Pattern Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy caused by distinct pattern labels representing the same master column.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a pattern master with column vectors \(a^p\), costs \(c_p\), and dual vector \(\pi\), suppose distinct patterns \(p_1,\ldots,p_k\) satisfy \(a^{p_j}=a\) and \(c_{p_j}=c\). Every duplicate then has the same reduced cost \(c-\pi^{\mathsf T}a\), and the master depends on their variables only through \(\sum_{j=1}^k x_{p_j}\). Consequently, any feasible redistribution preserving that sum preserves all master constraints and the objective, producing alternative representations and potentially degenerate pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identically composed, identically priced patterns are interchangeable; redistributing their total weight changes neither feasibility nor cost, creating symmetric master solutions.
assumptions_latex: The master is linear in the pattern variables.
Duplicate patterns have identical columns and costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar c_{p_1}=\cdots=\bar c_{p_k}=c-\pi^{\mathsf T}a,\qquad \sum_jx_{p_j}\ \text{alone determines their master contribution}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows directly from equality of columns and costs in a linear master formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Interchangeability of identical columns and costs is correct, but the further connection to degenerate pivots requires an authoritative column-generation or degeneracy source.

children.title: Pattern-Space Explosion
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial growth in the number of feasible cutting patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Pattern-Space Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit counting family for one-dimensional cutting patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(m\) item types, each of unit length, and stock length \(L\). A pattern is any vector \(a\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\le L\). Stars-and-bars gives exactly \(\binom{m+L}{L}\) feasible patterns. In particular, when \(m=L=n\), the pattern count is \(\binom{2n}{n}=\Theta(4^n/\sqrt n)\); hence explicit pattern enumeration requires exponential output size in this family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with unit lengths, the number of feasible patterns is a binomial coefficient and becomes exponential when the number of types and capacity grow together.
assumptions_latex: \(m,L\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
Patterns may leave unused stock.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|\mathcal P|=\binom{m+L}{L},\qquad |\mathcal P|=\Theta(4^n/\sqrt n)\ \text{when }m=L=n.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary stars-and-bars count with the standard central-binomial asymptotic

children.title: State-Space Explosion
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial growth in states used by network representations.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity boundary of capacity-indexed exact pricing states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacity-indexed dynamic program for one-dimensional knapsack pricing with integer capacity \(W\), the conventional exact state set contains one state for each residual or used capacity in \(\{0,\ldots,W\}\). Its table therefore has \(W+1\) capacity states and is pseudopolynomial in \(W\). If \(W=2^n\) is encoded in binary, its encoding uses \(n+1\) bits while the state count is \(2^n+1\), exponential in the capacity's bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacity-indexed exact dynamic program is pseudopolynomial: a binary-encoded capacity can induce exponentially many capacity states relative to its encoding length.
assumptions_latex: \(W\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) is binary encoded.
The dynamic program distinguishes every integral used or residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|S_W|=W+1;\qquad W=2^n\Longrightarrow |S_W|=2^n+1.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard pseudopolynomial capacity-state count under binary encoding

children.title: Compression Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance regimes where state aggregation provides limited size reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic obstruction to lossless compression of distinguishable patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a finite pattern family and let \(\phi:\mathcal P\to S\) be a compressed state map. If exact recovery of every pattern is required, so that a decoder \(D:S\to\mathcal P\) satisfies \(D(\phi(a))=a\) for all \(a\in\mathcal P\), then \(\phi\) is injective and \(|S|\ge|\mathcal P|\). For unit-length patterns with \(m\) types and capacity \(L\), this forces \(|S|\ge\binom{m+L}{L}\); no lossless state aggregation avoids the pattern-space explosion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If downstream constraints must recover every pattern exactly, compressed states must distinguish all patterns, so compression cannot reduce the worst-case state count.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is finite.
The compressed representation permits exact decoding of every pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D\circ\phi=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal P}\Longrightarrow |S|\ge|\mathcal P|;\qquad |S|\ge\binom{m+L}{L}\ \text{for unit-length patterns}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: injectivity follows from existence of a left inverse, combined with the elementary pattern count
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Fractional-Integer Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Fractional utilization that does not directly yield an integer plan.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Integer Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-item configuration-LP example exhibiting a strict integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take three distinct items of size \(1/2\) and bins of capacity \(1\). Include every singleton and pair configuration. Assign weight \(1/2\) to each of the three pair configurations and zero to singletons. Each item is fractionally covered exactly once, and the LP objective is \(3/2\). Any integer packing requires two bins, attained by one pair and one singleton. Thus the fractional configuration solution does not directly specify an integer packing and has gap \(2-3/2=1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three half-size items use 1.5 bins fractionally through half-weighted pairs, but every integer packing needs two bins.
assumptions_latex: Each item must be assigned exactly once.
A bin may contain at most two of the three items.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\frac32<2=z_{\mathrm{IP}}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Operationally Invalid Generated Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-feasible pattern invalidated by an omitted incompatibility restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two item types have widths \(w_1,w_2>0\) with \(w_1+w_2\le W\), but suppose the production process forbids placing both types in one stock object. Hence a column can be valid for the pricing relaxation yet invalid for the actual cutting process.

children.title: Knapsack to Bin Configuration

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack to Bin Configuration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-selection representation of a feasible bin configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given items \(i\in I\) with sizes \(s_i>0\) and bin capacity \(B>0\), a subset \(C\subseteq I\) is a feasible bin configuration exactly when its incidence vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in I}s_ix_i\le B\). Thus generating a configuration is a zero-one knapsack selection problem; with item values \(v_i\), a best configuration maximizes \(\sum_i v_ix_i\) subject to the same capacity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bin configuration is precisely a binary knapsack selection whose total item size does not exceed bin capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\text{ is feasible}\Longleftrightarrow x=\mathbf1_C\in\{0,1\}^{I}\text{ and }\sum_{i\in I}s_ix_i\le B.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack to Cutting Pattern

Consequently, maximizing a linear pattern value \(\sum_i v_i a_i\) is a bounded integer-knapsack problem; omitting the bounds gives the unbounded integer-knapsack form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional cutting pattern is an integer-knapsack selection of item multiplicities within the stock length and any type bounds.

\(u_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) when bounds are imposed.

children.title: Configuration Partitioning for Bin Packing

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Partitioning for Bin Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-partitioning formulation using feasible bin configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite item set and \(\mathcal C\) the family of capacity-feasible subsets of \(I\). For each \(C\in\mathcal C\), let \(y_C\in\{0,1\}\) indicate use of one bin containing exactly \(C\). Bin packing is represented by minimizing \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}y_C\) subject to \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C:i\in C}y_C=1\) for every \(i\in I\). The equalities partition the items among the selected configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bin packing selects feasible subsets as bins so that every individual item belongs to exactly one selected configuration.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
\(\mathcal C\) contains every capacity-feasible item subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min\left\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}y_C:\sum_{C\ni i}y_C=1\ \forall i\in I,\ y_C\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]

The inequalities allow overproduction while ensuring every demand is met.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Sum Reduction Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity reduction from SUBSET SUM to exact-fill pattern feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a SUBSET SUM instance with positive integers \(q_1,\ldots,q_n\) and target \(T\), construct one item of length \(q_i\) for each index and stock length \(T\). The construction copies the binary-encoded numbers and is computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset sums to the target exactly when the corresponding binary cutting or knapsack pattern fills stock of that target length without trim.

children.title: Partition Reduction Route

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Reduction Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction from PARTITION to two-bin packing with identical capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=2B\). Construct a bin-packing decision instance having one item of size \(a_i\) for every \(i\), two bins, and capacity \(B\) per bin. The items fit into the two bins if and only if there exists \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(\sum_{i\in S}a_i=B\). Thus this polynomial-time transformation transfers the weak NP-hardness of PARTITION to the two-bin packing decision problem when sizes and capacities are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition instance of total size twice the target is feasible exactly when its items fit into two bins of target capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for every \(i\).
\(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=2B\), with all integers binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed two-bin instance is feasible if and only if \(\exists S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:\sum_{i\in S}a_i=B\).

notation.meaning: target sum and capacity of each bin

children.title: Weak-Hardness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Complexity classification associated with arithmetic reduction routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Hardness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-versus-unary encoding boundary for the standard integral 0–1 knapsack decision problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\) items with nonnegative integral weights \(w_i\), nonnegative integral profits \(p_i\), capacity \(B\), and profit target \(P\), the 0–1 knapsack decision problem asks whether some \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in S}w_i\le B\) and \(\sum_{i\in S}p_i\ge P\). A capacity-indexed dynamic program solves this problem in \(O(nB)\) time and \(O(B)\) space. Thus it is polynomial-time when \(B\) is polynomially bounded in the input length, including when \(B\) is unary encoded, but pseudopolynomial under unrestricted binary encoding. Together with a standard PARTITION reduction, this gives the usual weak-NP-hardness boundary for binary-encoded 0–1 knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard integral 0–1 knapsack has an exact capacity-indexed algorithm using O(nB) time and O(B) space. This is polynomial for unary or otherwise polynomially bounded capacity but only pseudopolynomial for unrestricted binary capacity, matching its weak NP-hardness.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(w_i,p_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), and \(B,P\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\).
Arithmetic and table operations are counted as constant-time operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated 0–1 knapsack decision problem is solvable in \(O(nB)\) time and \(O(B)\) space, yielding a pseudopolynomial exact algorithm under binary encoding and a polynomial-time algorithm whenever \(B\) is polynomially bounded in the input length.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical capacity-indexed 0-1 knapsack dynamic program and encoding distinction

children.title: Three-Partition Route
children.top_down_role: The strong-hardness route for packing and stock-cutting families.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Partition Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-hardness reduction from restricted 3-PARTITION to bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a restricted 3-PARTITION instance contain \(3m\) positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_{3m}\) satisfying \(B/4<a_i<B/2\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^{3m}a_i=mB\). Create one bin-packing item of size \(a_i\) for each integer and ask whether all items fit into at most \(m\) bins of capacity \(B\). The packing instance is feasible if and only if the integers can be partitioned into \(m\) triples, each summing to \(B\). Because restricted 3-PARTITION is strongly NP-complete, this transformation establishes strong NP-hardness of bin packing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted 3-PARTITION is equivalent to packing its numbers into m capacity-B bins; the size bounds force every feasible bin to contain exactly three items.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(a_i,B\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(B/4<a_i<B/2\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The items fit into \(m\) bins of capacity \(B\) if and only if they admit a partition into \(m\) triples of sum \(B\); the resulting feasibility problem is strongly NP-hard.

notation.meaning: required triple sum and bin capacity

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical restricted 3-PARTITION reduction to bin packing

children.title: Pricing-Complexity Route
children.top_down_role: The dependence of implicit-column methods on their knapsack pricing problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Complexity Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact knapsack pricing characterization for the unit-cost cutting-stock master LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i a_i\le W\}\) be the set of feasible cutting patterns in a cutting-stock master LP, and suppose every pattern has cost \(1\). For nonnegative dual prices \(\pi_i\), the reduced cost of pattern \(a\in A\) is \(1-\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i a_i\). Therefore the pricing subproblem is the unbounded integer knapsack problem \[z(\pi)=\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i a_i:a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^n,\ \sum_{i=1}^n w_i a_i\le W\right\}.\] A negative-reduced-cost column exists if and only if \(z(\pi)>1\), so every exact pricing step requires deciding or optimizing this knapsack subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a unit-cost cutting-stock master problem, pricing maximizes dual value over nonnegative integer patterns that fit within the stock width. A negative-reduced-cost pattern exists exactly when the resulting unbounded-knapsack optimum exceeds one.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(w_i,W\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\pi_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in\{1,7d9,n\}\).
Every feasible cutting pattern has master-problem cost \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum pattern reduced cost is \(1-z(\pi)\); hence an improving pattern exists if and only if \(z(\pi)>1\), and exact pricing is an unbounded integer knapsack optimization problem.
